Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 46, verses 1–2:

Surat al-Ahqaf

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr that it was revealed in Makkah. Many scholars stated its Meccan status without exception, but some excepted His saying, ﴿Say: Have you considered, if it is from Allah...﴾ (verse 10). Al-Tabarani reported with a sound chain from 'Awf ibn Malik al-Ashja'i that it was revealed in Madinah concerning the conversion of 'Abdullah ibn Salam. This is also narrated from Muhammad ibn Sirin.

In *al-Durr al-Manthur*, al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas that he said: "I did not hear the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say to anyone walking on the face of the earth that he is among the people of Paradise, except 'Abdullah ibn Salam, and concerning him it was revealed: ﴿And a witness from the Children of Israel testified...﴾" (verse 10). There are many reports about its revelation concerning him, may Allah be pleased with him. The apparent meaning is that it is Madani, because his conversion occurred in it. Indeed, there are reports that indicate its Madani status from another angle. 'Ikrimah denies that it was revealed concerning him and says: "It is Meccan," as 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him. Likewise Masruq. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him that he said about the verse: "By Allah, it was not revealed concerning 'Abdullah ibn Salam. It was revealed only in Makkah. Ibn Salam's conversion occurred in Madinah. It was only a dispute in which Muhammad ﷺ argued." Some excepted ﴿And the one who said to his parents...﴾ (verse 17), two verses. "Marwan claimed that the Prophet ﷺ cursed his father while he was in his loins, and that these two verses were revealed concerning 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr, may Allah be pleased with them both. 'A'ishah contradicted him and said: 'Marwan lied twice. By Allah, it is not about him. If I wished to name the one about whom it was revealed, I would have named him. But the Messenger of Allah ﷺ cursed the father of Marwan, while Marwan was in his loins, so Marwan is a *fadadun*, i.e., a piece of the curse of Allah, the Exalted.'" In another report she said: "It was only revealed concerning so-and-so son of so-and-so," and she named another man. Another scholar excepted ﴿And We have enjoined upon man...﴾ (verses 15–18), the four verses, as related in *Jamal al-Qurra'*. He also related an exception for ﴿So be patient as the messengers of firm resolve were patient﴾ (verse 35). He transmitted this from *al-Bahr* on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah. Likewise, an exception concerning ﴿Say: Have you considered...﴾ etc. has been reported from them both. The full discussion of this will come, Allah willing.

Its verses number thirty-five according to the Kufan count and thirty-four according to others. The disagreement concerns *Ha Mim* (حم), and it is called "Thirty" because it exceeds thirty.

Ahmad reported with a good chain from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ taught me a surah from the Ha Mim group, which is al-Ahqaf. Whenever a surah exceeded thirty verses, it was named 'Thirty.' It is also reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited it in two ways."

Ibn al-Durays and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, reported from Ibn Mas'ud who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ taught me Surat al-Ahqaf. Then I heard a man reciting it differently from that. I said: 'Who taught you this?' He said: 'The Messenger of Allah ﷺ.' I said: 'By Allah, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ taught me other than this.' So we went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, did you not teach me such and such?' He said: 'Yes.' The other said: 'Did you not teach me such and such?' He said: 'Yes.' Then the face of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ changed and he said: '(Let each one of you recite what he has heard, for those before you were destroyed only by disagreement.)'"

You know that what is mass-transmitted (*mutawatir*) is the Qur'an. The connection of this surah: when Allah, the Exalted, concluded the previous surah with mention of monotheism, the censure of the people of polytheism, and the warning, He began this one with monotheism and then with rebuke of the disbelievers among the servants. Thus, He, Mighty and Majestic, said:

(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.)

﴿Ha Mim. The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ The discussion of this is like what preceded at the beginning of the previous surah.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 46, verse 3:

﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth﴾ with what is in them, in terms of their being parts of them and in terms of their being settled within them, ﴿and what is between them﴾ of the creatures, ﴿except with truth﴾. This is an exceptive (istithna' mufarragh) construction, from the most general of the objects (mafa'il), meaning: except as a creation joined with the truth which wisdom (al-hikmah) requires, both the cosmic (takwiniyyah) and the legislative (tashri'iyyah). In this there is, to no small degree, evidence for the existence of the Creator (al-Sani'), for the attributes of His perfection, and for the grounding of His acts upon profound wisdoms and their culmination in sublime ends.

It has also been permitted that it is an exceptive construction from the most general of the states (ahwal) relating to the subject of "We created" (khalaqna) or to its object, meaning: We did not create them in any state except the state of Our being joined with the truth, or the state of their being joined with it. ﴿and a specified term﴾ is conjoined to (al-Haqq) with an elided noun (mudaf), meaning: and with the determination of a specified term. It was necessary to posit the elision, because creation is joined with the term only in its relation to what is joined with it, not with the term itself. The intended meaning of this term, as Ibn 'Abbas said, is the Day of Resurrection, for all matters end at it, the earth is changed into other than the earth and the heavens likewise, and they come forth before God, the One, the Subduer. It has also been said: it is the duration of survival determined for each thing. The first view is supported by His statement, exalted is He: ﴿and those who disbelieve turn away from what they are warned of﴾, for what they were warned of is the Day of Resurrection and its complete catastrophe and its general terrors, not the end of their lifespans.

It has also been permitted that "ma" is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah), meaning: concerning their warning of that time, by the idafah of the verbal noun to its first object which takes the place of the subject. The clause is then circumstantial (haliyyah), meaning: We did not create the creation except with truth, and the appointed term at which they will be recompensed is determined, while the state is that they do not believe in it, turn away from it, and are not prepared for its arrival.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 46, verse 4:

﴿Say﴾ as a rebuke and reproach to them. ﴿Tell me﴾: inform me. It is also read as (أرَأيْتَكُمْ). ﴿What you invoke﴾: what you worship ﴿besides Allah﴾, namely the idols, or all false objects of worship. The latter is probably the more apparent meaning. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is the first object of (أرَأيْتُمْ). The words of the Exalted, ﴿Show me﴾, are an emphasis of it, since it also carries the meaning of "inform me." The words of the Exalted, ﴿what have they created﴾, admit several readings. (Ma) may be an interrogative noun, a fronted object of (خَلَقُوا), with (ذا) being superfluous. Or (ماذا) may be a single interrogative noun functioning as a fronted object, meaning "what thing have they created." Or (ما) may be an interrogative noun serving as subject or fronted predicate, with (ذا) a relative noun serving as predicate or delayed subject, and the clause (خَلَقُوا) is the relative clause, meaning "what is that which they created." In the first two readings, the clause (خَلَقُوا) is the second object of (أرَأيْتُمْ). In the readings after them, the clause is (ماذا خَلَقُوا). It is also admitted that the sentence belongs to the category of *i'mal* (the verb-government dispute), in which the second verb has been made to govern and the object of the first has been deleted. Abu Hayyan preferred this view. It has also been said that (أرُونِي) may be a *badal al-ishtimal* (inclusive substitute) of (أرَأيْتُمْ). Ibn 'Atiyya said: (أرَأيْتُمْ) admits two possibilities: that it is transitive with (ما) as its object, or that it is merely an attention-calling particle that does not take an object, with (ما) being interrogative, for the sake of rebuke. This second view was stated by al-Akhfash regarding the verse ﴿Did you see when we took refuge at the rock?﴾.

The words of the Exalted, ﴿from the earth﴾, explain the indefinite in ﴿what have they created﴾. It has been said that the apparent meaning is that it refers to the parts and patches of the earth. It is also admitted that it refers to what is upon its surface, of animals and other things, by way of an implied noun that conveys this meaning. It is also possible that "earth" refers to the lower things in general, and this is probably preferable. ﴿Or do they have a partnership﴾: that is, a partnership with Allah, glorified is He, ﴿in the heavens﴾: that is, in their creation. Probably it is also preferable to interpret "in them" as referring to the upper things. (Am) admits that it may be disjunctive (*munqati'a*) or conjunctive (*muttasila*). The intended meaning is the negation of their gods' entitlement to worship in the most complete manner. For first he negated their having any role, in truth and independently, in the creation of any part of the lower world. Second, he negated their having any role, by way of partnership, in the creation of any part of the upper world. It is known that negating this entails negating their entitlement to worship. The restriction of partnership in the sublime composition to the words of the Exalted, ﴿in the heavens﴾, although there is no partnership in them and in the earth as well, is because the purpose is to bind them to something that is conceded to them and apparent to everyone. Partnership in the lower events is not of this kind, since they possess and bring about some of them in the outward appearance. It has been said: the more apparent view is that the verse be taken as omitting the counterpart of the conjunctive (am), since its evidence is present, and the implied meaning is: "Do they have a partnership in the earth, or do they have a partnership in the heavens?" But this, as you see, is weak. The words of the Exalted, ﴿Bring me a Book﴾ to the end of the verse, are a rebuke to them by showing their incapacity to bring a transmitted proof, after rebuking them for their incapacity to bring a rational proof. It is therefore part of the speech, meaning: "Bring me a divine Book existing ﴿before﴾ this Book, that is, the Qur'an, which speaks of monotheism and the nullification of polytheism, and which indicates the soundness of your religion." ﴿Or a remnant of knowledge﴾: that is, a remainder of knowledge left to you from the knowledge of the ancients, testifying to their entitlement to worship. So *athara* is a verbal noun like *dalala*, meaning "remainder," from their saying: "The she-camel became fat with a remnant (*athara*) of meat," that is, a remainder of it.

Al-Qurtubi said: it means transmission and narration, and from it is the saying of al-A'sha:

*Indeed, what you two dispute about is clear to the listener and to the one who transmits.*

Abu Salama ibn 'Abd al-Rahman and Qatada said: the meaning is "or a special knowledge," and so its derivation is from *ithra* (preference), as if Allah, exalted is He, has given preference to those with whom it is. It has also been said that it means a sign. Ahmad, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted, by way of Abu Salama ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding ﴿or a remnant of knowledge﴾, that he said: "The writing (*al-khatt*)." This is also related as a statement of Ibn 'Abbas himself (*mawquf*), and it has been interpreted as the knowledge of *al-raml* (geomancy), as in the hadith of Abu Hurayra traced to the Prophet (ﷺ):

"There was a prophet among the prophets who used to draw lines in the sand; whoever happened to hit upon a line like his line, he would know."

And in a report from the scholar (*al-Habr*, i.e., Ibn 'Abbas) he said: ﴿or a remnant of knowledge﴾ means "a line that the Arabs used to draw in the earth." This clearly supports the cause of the science of geomancy, and that it has some validity and points to some matters. There is discussion of this in its proper place. In *al-Bahr* it is said: if Ibn 'Abbas's interpretation of *athara* as writing on dust is sound, then that is by way of mockery of them, their statements, and their proofs. The tanwin (nunation) of (أثارَةٍ) is for diminution. The phrase ﴿of knowledge﴾ is a qualifier, meaning: "or bring me a small remnant existing from knowledge." ﴿If you are truthful﴾ in your claim. For such a thing is hardly sound unless a rational proof or a transmitted proof supports it. Since neither of these supports it, and both stand against it, its falsity is made clear.

It is read as (إثارَةٍ) with a kasra on the hamza, and it has been interpreted as "debate," for it stirs up meanings (*tuthiru al-ma'ani*). It has been said: this is a metaphor, comparing what is brought out and made manifest by debate to the dust raised by the movements of horsemen. 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them, read it with a variant from one of them. Zayd ibn 'Ali, 'Ikrima, Qatada, al-Hasan, al-Sulami, al-A'mash, and 'Amr ibn Maymun read (أثَرَةٍ) without an alif, and it is the singular whose plural is (أُثُرٌ), like (قَتَرَةٍ) and (قُتُرٍ). 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, al-Sulami, and Qatada also read it with a sukun on the thaa, and it is the single act of what is transmitted, meaning: "you have been content from me with a single report or a single transmitted matter that testifies to the soundness of your statement." It is related from al-Kisa'i that he read the hamza with a damma and the thaa with a sukun, so it is a noun of quantity, like (غَرْفَةٍ) for what is scooped with the hand, meaning: "bring me something of knowledge that is transmitted." It is also related from him that he read (إثْرَةٍ) with a kasra on the hamza and a sukun on the thaa, and it has the meaning of (أثَرَةٍ) with two fathas.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 46, verse 5:

﴿And who is more astray than one who calls upon other than Allah, such as will not respond to him﴾. This is a denial that they could be more astray than the polytheists. Some of the virtuous scholars mentioned that the intended meaning is the negation that anyone could equal them in error, although the construction (*sabk al-tarkib*) is for negating that anything could be more astray. What relates to this has already passed, so recall it. That is, he is more astray than every astray person, since he abandoned calling upon the One who responds, the capable one who combines all the attributes of perfection, as the majestic Name indicates, and called upon one whose nature is not to respond to him or to grant his request, ﴿until the Day of Resurrection﴾. That is, for as long as the world lasts. Its apparent meaning is that after it, a response will occur, but this is not intended, since there is clear evidence to the contrary. This limit (*ghaya*), according to what is in *al-Intisaf*, is among the limits that indicate that what follows it, although it agrees with what precedes it, is nevertheless so much greater in a clear way that it joins it with the opposite, so that the two states, though they are one type, are like a thing and its opposite because of the difference between them. This is because the first state, whose limit is made the Resurrection, does not exceed non-response, whereas the second state, which is in the Resurrection, exceeds non-response by enmity and by disbelief in their worship of them, as what follows it makes clear. So it belongs to the same category as His saying, Exalted is He, in Surat al-Zukhruf: ﴿Nay, I gave enjoyment to these and their fathers﴾, to the end of the verse, and similar to it is His saying, glorified is He, concerning Iblis: ﴿And indeed upon you is My curse until the Day of Judgment﴾. It may also be said that what is intended by this limit is perpetuity, as was said concerning His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿abiding therein as long as the heavens endure﴾, and the saying of the Arabs: "as long as Thabir endures" (Thabir being a mountain). Some of them said: there is no difficulty in the verse, because the limit is an implicit meaning (*mafhum*), so it does not contradict the explicit meaning (*manTuq*). But this is open to discussion, for in *al-Durar* and *al-Yanbu'*, citing *al-Badi'*, it is stated that the limit, according to us, is of the kind of the indication of the text (*isharat al-nass*), not an implicit meaning.

Al-Zarkashi said in his commentary on *Jam' al-Jawami'*: Al-Qadi Abu Bakr [al-Baqillani] held that the ruling regarding the limit is explicit, and he claimed that the people of the language stated clearly that the attachment of a ruling to a limit is set up so that what follows it is contrary to what precedes it, because they agreed that it is not an independent statement. For His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿until she marries another husband﴾ and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿until they are purified﴾ require an implied element to complete the sentence. That implied element is either the opposite of what precedes it or not, and the latter is impossible, because nothing in the speech indicates it. So it is estimated as: "until they are purified, then approach them," and "until she marries another husband, so that she becomes lawful." He said: the implied element has the status of the explicit, since it is only implied because it comes first to the mind of one who knows the language. On this the Hanafi author of *al-Badi'* proceeded, and he said: it is according to us from the indication of the expression, not from the implicit meaning; but the majority hold that it is an implicit meaning, and they deny that the language is set up for that. End of quotation. From this it is known that his statement in *al-Talwih*, that the implicit meaning of the limit is agreed upon, is not free from flaw.

﴿And they, of their calling, are heedless﴾. The first pronoun refers to the object of (*yad'u*, "calls"), namely ﴿such as will not respond﴾, and the second refers to its subject. The plural in both is by consideration of the meaning of (*man*, "who"), just as the singular in what preceded is by consideration of its form. That is: those who call upon those who will not respond to them are heedless of their calling them. ﴿Heedless﴾: they do not hear and they are not aware. As for if the one called upon is inanimate, it is obvious. As for if he is of those endowed with reason: if he is among those accepted and brought near to Allah, Exalted is He, then it is because he is occupied from that by the good he is in; or because he is in a place that is not of the kind where the one in it hears the caller's call, due to distance, like Jesus, upon him be peace, today; or because Allah, Exalted is He, protects his hearing from hearing that, since, being of what does not please Allah, Exalted is He, it would pain him if he heard it. And if he is among the enemies of Allah, Exalted is He, such as the devils of jinn and men who were worshipped besides Allah, Exalted is He, then if he is dead, it is because he is occupied with the evil he is in. It was also said: because it is not the nature of the dead to hear, and no hearing can be realized from him except by a miracle, like the hearing of the people of the well. There is a discussion of this, part of which has passed. And if he is alive: if he is far away, for example, the matter is clear. If he is near and of sound faculties, it was said: the speech concerning him is after interpreting heedlessness as not hearing, and it is by way of prevalence (*taghlib*), because this category is rare.

Some people interpreted the heedlessness as lack of benefit, and it was objected that then the description of them as heedless after the description of them as not responding would have little benefit. Some considered the prevalence without interpretation, in the sense that what is prevalent is the one to whom heedlessness is truly attributed over others. This is like the prevalence in referring to those deities with what is by convention used for rational beings. Although the verse concerns worshippers of idols and the like, which do not reason, the attribution of heedlessness is figurative, and the expression with what is for the rational is for the worshippers' treating them in the manner of rational beings.

Some said, on the view that the verse concerns worshippers of idols: if it describes them with what was mentioned, namely non-response and heedlessness, while their condition is manifest, it is for mockery of them. So reflect, and do not be heedless.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 46, verse 6:**

﴿And when mankind is gathered﴾ at the establishment of the Resurrection, ﴿they will be enemies to them﴾, meaning the objects of worship to their worshippers, ﴿intensely hostile﴾. ﴿And they will deny their worship﴾, meaning the objects of worship also, ﴿by their worship﴾, i.e., by the unbelievers' worship of them, ﴿disbelieving﴾, meaning rejecting. The matter is evident regarding rational beings. As for idols, it has been narrated that God Most High creates for them perception and makes them speak, so they disavow their worshippers' worship, and likewise they will be enemies to them. It is also permitted that the denial of the idols be by the tongue of their state (bi-lisan al-hal), because it is clear that they are not fit for worship and that they have no benefit for them, as the worshippers had imagined at first when they said: ﴿We only worship them that they may bring us nearer to Allah﴾, and they hoped for their intercession. The enmity has been interpreted as harm, on the basis that it is a metonymy of the type majaz mursal (figurative usage with a non-resemblance relation) from it. Thus the meaning of ﴿they will be enemies to them﴾ is that they will be harmful to them. What we have mentioned in explaining the pronouns is the apparent meaning. It has been said that the pronoun (hum), both the explicit and the implicit pronoun in the words of God Most High, ﴿and they are heedless of their supplication﴾, refers to the unbelievers who call upon them, and the pronoun in ﴿their supplication﴾ refers to them, or to the objects of worship. The meaning is that the unbelievers are heedless of their error, in that they call upon one who does not respond to them, and they do not reflect on what is upon them in that. There is in this, from the committing of what is contrary to the apparent meaning, what there is, and in the pronouns after such. The meaning, when mankind is gathered, is that the unbelievers will be enemies to their false deities, because of what they see of the punishment resulting from worshipping them, and they will, for that reason, deny that they worshipped other than God Most High, as God Most High related of them, that they say: ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾. It has been objected that the context is for the explanation of the state of the deities with them, not the reverse, and because their unbelief at that time is a denial of their worship, and calling it unbelief is contrary to the apparent meaning.

[Page 8]

﴿And when Our verses are recited to them as clear proofs﴾ means clear, or making clear what needs to be made clear. ﴿those who disbelieved say of the truth﴾ means the verses being recited. The verses are referred to by the noun "the truth" in place of a pronoun (ḍamīr), to specify their truthfulness and the obligation to believe in them. In the same way, the phrase "those recited to them" is replaced by the description "those who disbelieved," to record upon them complete disbelief and misguidance.

It is also permitted that "the truth" refers to prophethood (nubuwwah) or to Islam. In that case, the phrase is not a substitute for a pronoun. The first interpretation is more apparent. The particle lām (lām al-ʿillah, the particle of causation) is connected to "say," meaning they said it on account of the truth and concerning it. What is said about something is said because of it. It is also permitted that the lām is connected to "disbelieved," in the sense of the particle bāʾ, or that disbelief is understood as its opposite, belief (īmān), which takes the lām in constructions like ﴿Shall we believe you?﴾. This is contrary to the apparent meaning, as is not hidden.

﴿when it came to them﴾ means at the time of its coming to them. Customarily, this implies hastening, which entails the absence of reflection and contemplation. It is as if it were said: they rushed at the first hearing of the truth without reflection, to the point that they said: ﴿This is clear magic.﴾ That is, it is evident that it is magic. Their judgment of this applies to the verses because of their inability to produce the like of them, and to prophethood because of the miraculous (khāriq lil-ʿādah, that which breaks the normal course of nature) that accompanies it, and to Islam because it separates a man from his wife and his child.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 46, verse 8:

﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ This is a turning away (idrab) and a transition (intiqal) from relating their previous abomination to relating something even more abominable, namely lying deliberately against God, exalted and majestic is He. For lying, especially against Him, mighty and majestic, is agreed upon as being ugly, to the extent that you see everyone recoiling from attributing it to Him. This is unlike magic, for although it is ugly, it does not reach this degree, such that its knowledge is almost counted among desirable matters. In the interrogative "am" (am al-munqati'ah, the disjunctive "am") there is the hamza with the meaning of reproachful denial, containing amazement at attributing it to invention, together with their saying: "It is magic," because of their inability to produce its like. As for the pronoun in ﴿invented it﴾ (iftarahu), as Abu Hayyan said, it refers to ﴿the truth﴾ which is the recited verses. Some of them said: it refers to the Qur'an, which is indicated by what preceded, that is, "Or do they say, 'He has invented it'?"

﴿Say: If I have invented it﴾ on the assumption, ﴿then you control nothing for me from God in any respect.﴾ That is, God, exalted is He, would have hastened to punish me for inventing against Him, glory be to Him, so you would not be able to restrain Him, mighty and majestic, from dealing with me, nor could you bear to repel any part of His punishment, glory be to Him, from me. So how would I invent it and expose myself to His punishment? Thus the answer to "if" (in) is in reality omitted, and it is "He would have hastened to punish me," and what is mentioned is its consequence, placed in its stead, or used figuratively for it. ﴿He is most knowing of what you plunge into﴾ — of that which you take up of disparagement of the revelation of God, exalted is He, and of slandering His verses, and calling it magic at one time and invention at another. The use of ifada (plunging) for taking up and beginning something, whether by speech or action, is a well-known metaphor; its original sense is the pouring out of water, as one says: afada al-ma'a (he poured out the water) when he caused it to flow. What we have indicated, that "ma" is a relative pronoun and the pronoun in "fihi" returns to it, is the apparent reading, but it is also permitted that "ma" be a verbal-source (masdariyyah) particle and the pronoun in "fihi" refer to the truth or to the Qur'an.

﴿Sufficient is He as a witness between me and you﴾ — He, glory be to Him, bears witness for me to truthfulness and delivery of the message, and against you for lying and denial. This is a threat of recompense for your plunging into slander of the verses. It is stated as a new sentence (isti'naf) because it answers an assumed question. "Bihi" (with Him) is in the position of the subject of "kafa" (sufficed), according to the most correct opinions; "shahidan" (as a witness) is a circumstantial accusative (hal); and "bayni wa baynakum" (between me and you) is related either to it or to "kafa."

﴿And He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ — a promise of forgiveness and mercy for whoever repents and believes, and an indication of God's forbearance toward them, since He did not hasten to punish them and gave them respite, glory be to Him, so that they might amend their affairs.

**[Page 9]**

**(Al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on Surah 46, verse 9)**

﴿Say, "I am not a novelty among the messengers"﴾ That is, not a novel one among them. Meaning: I am not an innovator of a matter that contradicts their affairs; rather, I have brought what they brought, the call to monotheism (tawhid). Or: I have done similar to what they did, by manifesting the miracles that Allah the Exalted has given me, without bringing all the things that were proposed. It has been said that they used to propose to him, peace and blessings be upon him, wondrous signs and ask him about unseen matters, out of obstinacy and arrogance, so he, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, was commanded to say this to them.

The parallel of *bidʻan* (بِدْعًا) is *al-khiff* (الخِفُّ) in the sense of *al-khafif* (the light one), and *al-khill* (الخِلُّ) in the sense of *al-khalil* (the close friend). It is then a *sifah mushabbahah* (an adjective of quality, a grammatical term for a derived adjective), or a verbal noun interpreted as such. It has been permitted to keep it in its original form. ʻIkrimah, Abu Haywah and Ibn Abi ʻAblah recited (بَدَعًا) with a fatḥah on the dāl, and it is explained as the plural of *bidʻah* (بِدْعَةٍ), like *sidrah* and *sadar*, and the sentence is then (understood) with an elided genitive construction, meaning "one possessing novelties," or as a verbal noun, and the predication with it is for emphasis, or with the elision of the genitive construction as well.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible for it to be an adjective of the form *fiʻl*, as in their saying *dīnun qayyimun* (دِينٌ قَيِّمٌ, an upright religion) and *laḥmun zaymun* (لَحْمٌ زَيْمٌ), meaning scattered. Abu Hayyan said in *al-Bahr*: Sibawayh did not affirm an adjective on this pattern except for *ʻudiyy* (عُدِّيَ), when he said: "We do not know it to have come as an adjective except in a weak-lettered word describing a plural, which is *qawmun ʻudiyy*." He noted *zaym* as an exception, and this is a sound exception. As for *qayyim* (قَيِّمٌ), it is a shortened form from *qiyām*, and were it not so, its middle radical would have remained sound, as it did in *ḥiwal* and *ʻiwaḍ*. As for the saying of the Arabs: *makānun sawiyyun* (مَكانٌ سَوِيٌّ), *māʼun rawiyyun* (ماءٌ رَوِيٌّ), *rajulun riḍan* (رَجُلٌ رِضًا) and *māʼun ṣaran* (ماءٌ صَرًى), these are interpreted by the grammarians of morphology either as verbal nouns or as shortened forms. From Mujahid and Abu Haywah (also recited as) (بَدِعًا) with a fatḥah on the bāʼ and a kasrah on the dāl, and it is an adjective like *ḥadhir* (حَذِرٍ).

﴿Nor do I know what will be done with me or with you﴾ That is, in the two abodes, in detail, as has been said. Ibn Jarir reported from al-Hasan that he said regarding the verse: As for the Hereafter, then far be it (from Allah); he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, knew that he would be in Paradise when Allah took the covenant from him among the messengers. But he did not know what would be done with him in this world: whether he would be expelled as the prophets before him were expelled, or be killed as the prophets before him were killed; and not with you, my community, the one that denies, or my community, the one that affirms, or my community that is stoned with stones from the sky, or the one swallowed up by the earth. Then it was revealed to him: ﴿And [remember] when We said to you, "Indeed, your Lord has encompassed the people"﴾. He, the Exalted, says:

"I have secured for you from the Arabs that they will not kill you." So he, peace and blessings be upon him, knew that he would not be killed. Then Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿It is He who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth to make it prevail over all religion, and sufficient is Allah as a witness﴾. He says: He bore witness for you in His own self that He will make your religion prevail over the (other) religions. Then He, the Exalted, said to him, peace and blessings be upon him, concerning his community: ﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them, nor would Allah punish them while they seek forgiveness﴾. So Allah the Exalted informed him of what He did to him and what He would do to his community.

It is reported from al-Kalbi that the companions of the Prophet, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, said to him when they had become distressed by the harm of the polytheists: "How long shall we remain in this state?" He said: "Nor do I know what will be done with me or with you: whether I will be left in Mecca, or whether I will be commanded to leave for a land that has been shown to me and I have seen it," meaning in his dream, "with palm trees and trees."

In *al-Bahr* it is related from Malik ibn Anas, Qatadah, ʻIkrimah, al-Hasan as well, and Ibn ʻAbbas that the meaning is: what will be done with me or with you in the Hereafter.

Abu Dawud, in his book on abrogation (*Nasikh*), reported through ʻIkrimah from Ibn ʻAbbas that he said regarding the verse: It was abrogated by the verse: ﴿That Allah may forgive you your past and future sins﴾. So he, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, went out to the people and gave them the good news that Allah had forgiven him his past and future sins. A man among the believers said: "Congratulations to you, O Prophet of Allah! Now we know what will be done with you; so what will be done with us?" Then Allah the Exalted revealed in Surah al-Ahzab: ﴿And give good tidings to the believers that for them there is from Allah a great bounty﴾. And He, the Exalted, said: ﴿That He may admit the believing men and believing women into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein eternally, and remove from them their misdeeds﴾. So Allah the Exalted made clear what would be done to him and to them.

Concerning the authenticity of this report, it has been raised as an objection that abrogation does not apply to a statement of information (*khabar*). Perhaps what was abrogated is the command in His saying, the Exalted: (Say) [قُلْ], if we say that it is here for repetition, or the intended meaning of abrogation is general change.

Abu Hayyan said: This view is not apparent. Rather, Allah the Exalted had already informed His Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, from the beginning of his mission of his own state, the state of the believer, and the state of the disbeliever in the Hereafter. The Imam (al-Razi) said: Most of the scholars of verification have deemed this view improbable and argued that a prophet must know from himself that he is a prophet, and once he knows that, he knows that major sins do not proceed from him and that he is forgiven. And if that is so, it is impossible for him to be in doubt as to whether he is forgiven or not. Also, there is no doubt that the prophets are higher in rank than the saints, and Allah the Exalted has said concerning them: ﴿Unquestionably, the allies of Allah – there is no fear concerning them, nor will they grieve﴾. So how can it be believed that the Messenger, who is the chief of the prophets and the exemplar of the saints, would remain in doubt as to whether he is among those forgiven or not?

It may also be said: the intended meaning is also that he, peace and blessings be upon him, did not know that in detail. What was mentioned does not necessitate the attainment of detailed knowledge, since it is possible that he, peace and blessings be upon him, had been informed of that at the beginning of the matter in summary. Rather, informing him, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, of the state of each individual in detail is far-fetched, such that he would have been informed, peace and blessings be upon him, of the states of Zayd, for example, in the Hereafter in detail, and of the states of ʻAmr likewise, and so on. Here I pause.

In *Sahih al-Bukhari*, and it was narrated by Imam Ahmad, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Mardawayh, from Umm al-ʻAla', who had pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, that she said when ʻUthman ibn Maz'un died: "The mercy of Allah the Exalted be upon you, O Abu al-Sa'ib. My testimony for you is that Allah the Exalted has honored you." The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said: ("And how do you know that Allah the Exalted has honored him? As for him, certainty has come to him from his Lord, and I indeed hope good for him. By Allah, I do not know, and I am the Messenger of Allah, what will be done with me or with you.") Umm al-ʻAla' said: "By Allah, I shall never after this declare anyone pure (in this manner)."

In a narration of Ibn Hibban and al-Tabarani from Zayd ibn Thabit: "When he (ʻUthman) passed away, she said: 'Be at ease, O Abu al-Sa'ib, for you are in Paradise.' The Prophet, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, said: 'And how do you know?' She said: 'O Messenger of Allah, ʻUthman ibn Maz'un (said so)?' He said: 'Indeed, and we have seen nothing but good. By Allah, I do not know what will be done with me.'"

In a narration of al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh from Ibn ʻAbbas: "When he died, his wife, or a woman, said: 'Congratulations to you, Ibn Maz'un, for Paradise.' The Messenger of Allah, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, looked at her with an angry look and said: 'And how do you know? By Allah, I am the Messenger of Allah, and I do not know what Allah will do with me.' She said: 'O Messenger of Allah, your companion and your knight, and you know best!' He said: 'I hope for him the mercy of his Lord, the Exalted, and I fear his sin for him.'"

However, in this narration, Ibn ʻAbbas said: "And that was before the revelation of: ﴿That Allah may forgive you your past and future sins﴾."

From al-Dahhak: The meaning is: I do not know what I am commanded to do, nor what you are commanded to do, in matters of obligations, legislation, jihad, or trial and testing.

What I choose is that the meaning, in negating knowledge, is from a source other than revelation, whether the knowledge is detailed or summary, and whether that concerns worldly or otherworldly affairs. And I believe that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not depart from this world until he was given knowledge of Allah the Exalted, His attributes and His affairs, and knowledge of things whose knowledge is considered perfection, which no one else among the worlds was given. I do not believe that perfection is lost by not knowing particular worldly events, such as not knowing what Zayd, for example, is doing in his house or what will happen to him in his day or tomorrow. Nor do I consider it good for someone to say: "He, peace and blessings be upon him, knows the unseen." I find it better to say instead: "Allah the Exalted made him aware of the unseen," or "Allah the Exalted taught him it," or something similar.

In the verse there is a refutation of those who attribute to some of the saints the knowledge of everything, universal and particular. I have heard a preacher on the pulpit of the Friday mosque attributed to Shaykh ʻAbd al-Qadir al-Kilani, may his secret be sanctified, on a Friday, saying in a loud voice: "O falcon, you know me better than I know myself." And someone said to me: "I believe that the Shaykh, may his secret be sanctified, knows everything about me, even the roots of my hair." Things like this should not be attributed to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, so how could they be attributed to anyone other than him? Let the servant fear his Master.

In the reports that preceded concerning ʻUthman ibn Maz'un there is also a refutation of those who say of someone lower than him in merit, or of someone whom the truthful one (the Prophet) did not give the good news of Paradise and honor, similar to what has been said about him. Yes, a good opinion of the believers should be held, both living and dead, and hope for good for each of them, for Allah the Exalted is the Most Merciful of the merciful.

This is the apparent reading: that *mā* (ما) is an interrogative, in the nominative case by virtue of being the subject (*mubtadaʼ*), and the sentence after it is the predicate, and the subject-predicate clause is suspended (*muʻallaq*, a grammatical term for a verb whose effect is blocked by an interrogative, here the heart-verb) from it. The heart-verb (*al-fiʻl al-qalbi*, the verb of mental knowing) is either transitive to one object or two. It has been permitted for *mā* to be a relative pronoun in the accusative position as the object of the verb of knowing, and in that case it is transitive to one object, and the sentence after it is a relative clause. It has also been permitted for it to be a verbal particle (*ḥarf maṣdariyy*), in which case the verbal noun is the object of *adrī* (أدْرِي), and the interrogative is more fitting to the requirement of the context of disclaiming knowledge. And (*lā*) is for emphasizing the negation which extends over ﴿what will be done﴾ etc. and for reinforcing it. Were it not for considering the extension of the negation, the construction would have been *mā yufʻalu bī wa-bikum* without (*lā*), because it is not a place for negation nor for the extra use of *lā*. A parallel to this is the extra use of (*min*) in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Those who disbelieve among the People of the Book, nor the polytheists, would like that any good should be sent down upon you﴾, because of the extension of the (negation to) the desire, for when the desire for the sending down is negated, the sending down is negated. And the extra use of the *bāʼ* in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Do they not see that Allah, who created the heavens and the earth and was not wearied by their creation, is Able to bring the dead to life?﴾ is because of the extension of the negation, and also because *maʻa* (مَعَ) with what is within its scope is there; and were it not for it, the *bāʼ* would not have been added to the predicate. It has been said: the original is *wa-lā mā yafʻalu bikum*, and it was elided. It has also been said: *wa-lā bikum*. Zayd ibn ʻAli and Ibn Abi ʻAblah recited (yafʻalu) with the active voice, and its subject is the pronoun of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿I only follow what is revealed to me﴾ That is: I do not do anything except follow what is revealed to me, in the sense of restricting his actions, peace and blessings be upon him, to following revelation. The word "act" (*fiʻl*) here includes speech and other things. This is an answer to their proposal that he inform them of the unseen matters that had not been revealed to him, peace and blessings be upon him. The preceding address was to the polytheists.

It has been said: (this verse is) about the desire of the Muslims to be delivered from the harm of the polytheists, and the preceding address was to them. The first view is more suitable to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And I am not but a warner﴾, warning you of the punishment of Allah the Exalted as is revealed to me, ﴿clear﴾, clear in warning with the striking miracles. The restriction is relative. Ibn ʻUmayr recited (yūḥā) with the active voice.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 46, verse 10:

﴿Say: "Have you considered, if it is from Allah"﴾: that is, what is revealed to me of the Qur'an. It has also been said:

The pronoun refers to the Messenger. Against this view is that the apparent meaning, if it were intended, would be "I would be from Allah," not "sorcery or fabrication, as you claim," and ﴿and you disbelieve in it﴾.

The *waw* is for the circumstantial clause, and the clause is a circumstantial phrase with *qad* implied, according to the well-known view, regarding the pronoun in the predicate. It was placed between the parts of the condition for emphasis on their disbelief. Or the *waw* is for conjunction with *kana* ("if it is"), as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Have you considered, if it is from Allah, and you disbelieve in it﴾. Similarly is the *waw* in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿and a witness from the Children of Israel testified﴾. However, it conjoins it with what it was conjoined to, against the clause before it. So the clauses mentioned after the *waws* are not conjoined in a single sequence. Rather, the whole of "testified, then believed, and you were arrogant" is conjoined to the whole of "it is" and what accompanies it. Its like is in the words ﴿He is the First and the Last, and the Outward and the Inward﴾. The meaning is: if its being from Allah, Exalted is He, combines with your disbelief, and the testimony of the witness combines with his belief, along with your arrogance against belief... The discussion of the answer to the condition and of the two objects of *ara'aytum* will come, Allah willing, later.

The pronoun in ﴿in it﴾ refers to what the subject of *kana* refers to, which is what is revealed of the Qur'an or the Messenger. It is reported from al-Sha'bi that it refers to the Messenger. Perhaps he also says the pronoun in *kana* is likewise, and we say the pronoun in ﴿like it﴾ is so, to avoid disjunction.

You know that the apparent meaning is that all the pronouns return to the Qur'an. The indefiniteness of ﴿witness﴾ is for magnification, and likewise its description by the prepositional phrase, meaning: a witness of great standing from the Children of Israel, who stand upon the affairs of Allah, Exalted is He, and the secrets of revelation, by what they were given of the Torah, like the Qur'an in meanings contained in the Torah: of monotheism, promise, threat, and other things. For these are in reality the very same as what is in it, as His words, Exalted is He, indicate: ﴿And indeed it is in the scriptures of the former peoples﴾ in one respect. Likewise His words, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed this is in the former scrolls﴾. The likeness is in terms of its being conveyed in other expressions, or in terms of the like of what was mentioned, namely its being from Allah, Exalted is He, and the likeness is with respect to what was mentioned. It has been said: "like its testimony," that is, its testimony for itself that it is from Allah, Exalted is He, as if, by its inimitability, it testifies to itself with that. It has also been said: "like" is a metonymy for the Qur'an itself, for emphasis. And on the assumption that the pronoun refers to the Messenger, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, he interpreted "like" as Musa (peace be upon him).

Page 12

The *fa'* in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿so he believed﴾, that is, in the Qur'an, is causal, so that his belief is consequent upon a testimony to it for conforming to revelation. It may also be elaborative, so that his belief in it is itself the testimony for it. The meaning, on the assumption that what is intended is "so he believed in the Messenger, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him," is apparent with minimal consideration. His words, Exalted is He: ﴿and you were arrogant﴾, that is, toward belief, are conjoined to what we have pointed to, upon "a witness testified." It is also permitted that it be conjoined to "believed," since it is its counterpart, and the whole is conjoined to the condition. There is no repetition in ﴿you were arrogant﴾, because the arrogance is after the testimony and the disbelief is before it. His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾, that is, those characterized by this description, is an explanatory resumptive clause in the context of giving the cause for the arrogance toward belief. Describing them with wrongdoing serves to indicate the reason for the ruling. This clause thus indicates that their disbelief in it is due to their misguidance, which is caused by their wrongdoing. It is the evidence for the answer to the condition, and therefore it was omitted. The two objects of *ara'aytum* are also omitted, because the meaning indicates them. The estimate is: "Have you considered your state, if it is so? Then you have wronged, are you not wrongdoers?" So the first object is "your state," and the second is "are you not wrongdoers?" and the answer is "then you have wronged."

Ibn Atiyyah said: regarding *ara'aytum*, it may be a term of attention; it is a word established for asking and does not require an object. It may also be that the clause "if it is" etc. occupies the place of its two objects, but this is contrary to what the scholarly grammarians established on this. Al-Zamakhshari estimated the answer as "are you not wrongdoers?" without an *fa'*. Abu Hayyan refuted him, saying that when an interrogative clause occurs as the answer to a condition, the *fa'* must accompany it. If the particle is the hamza, it is placed before the *fa'*; otherwise it is placed after. Perhaps this is an estimate of meaning, not an estimate of i'rab (grammatical analysis). Some estimated it as "then will you believe?" for the indication of "so he believed." Al-Hasan estimated it as "then who is more astray than you?" in light of His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Have you considered, if it is from Allah, and you disbelieve in it, who is more astray than one who is in extreme opposition?"﴾ and His words, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾. It has been said: the estimate is "then who among us and you is the one upon truth, and who is the one upon falsehood?" It has been said: "you will perish." It has been said: it is ﴿so he believed and you were arrogant﴾, that is, "then Muhammad (ﷺ) has believed in it," or "the witness" and "you were arrogant" is yours, against belief. Most of these, as you see, are of this kind.

The witness is Abdullah ibn Salam, may Allah be pleased with him, according to the majority, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah, Ibn Sirin, al-Dahhak, and Ikrimah, in a report of Ibn Sa'd and Ibn Asakir from him. In the *Kashf* (of al-Zamakhshari), there is a discussion on making him the witness and the surah being Meccan, and for this reason I excepted this verse. Its verification is that what would be is set down as though it were actual, and for this reason "testified" and what follows it are conjoined to His words, Exalted is He: ﴿if it is from Allah and you disbelieve﴾, so that it is known that it is like it in verification, and it is in the manner of His words, glorified is He: ﴿as We sent down upon the dividers﴾, that is, He warned Quraysh with the like of what We sent down upon the Jews of Banu Qurayzah. And it was sent down upon them seven years after the descent of the verse. The point of the argument in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿so he believed﴾ is as if it were said: "Tell me: if a learned one from the Children of Israel believes in it" that is, one learned in what has been established for him, that it is like the Torah, "will you not be the most astray of people?" So there is in it the indication that it is like the Torah, and belief in it is obligatory, whether that witness testified or did not testify. For that testimony is followed by belief without delay, so if he did not believe, he would not be knowledgeable of what is in the Torah. This is suitable as an independent answer without regard to the first. As for the statement of one who said: "The witness is Abdullah," on this basis it is an explanation of the actual event, and that he was among those who testified and believed, not that the intended meaning of the verse's wording is Abdullah specifically. On both views, the statement of Sa'd must be interpreted. It has already been mentioned in the hadith of the two Shaykhs and others, and in it: "It was sent down, 'and a witness testified'," with the meaning being about his matter which would occur, according to the first view, or about it and about whoever is in his state. As if it were said: he is among those sent down concerning it, because he was among the witnesses. End of quotation.

It has been objected to his statement, "it is as though what would be were set down as actual," that there is no need for that descent according to its being Meccan, and that the witness is Ibn Salam, because of the conjunction upon the condition, by which the past becomes future. In that case, there is no harm in the witness's testimony after its descent. Nevertheless, the apparent meaning of the reports is that the descent was in Medina, and that it was after the testimony of Ibn Salam.

Abu Ya'la, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim reported with a sound chain, from Awf ibn Malik al-Ashja'i, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) set out, and I was with him, until we entered the synagogue of the Jews on their feast day. They disliked our entering upon them. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: 'Show me twelve men from among you who testify that there is no god but Allah, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and Allah will cause to perish from every Jew under the canopy of heaven the anger that is upon him.' They were silent, and none of them answered him. Then he repeated it to them, peace be upon him, and no one answered him. He repeated it a third time, and no one answered him. He said: 'You have refused. By Allah, I am the Gatherer, I am the Successor, and I am the Last. Either you believe or you deny.' Then the Prophet (ﷺ) departed, and I was with him, until we almost went out. Then there was a man behind him who said: 'Stay as you are, O Muhammad!' So he turned, and that man said: 'What sort of man do you know me to be among you, O company of Jews?' They said: 'By Allah, we know of no man among us more knowledgeable of the Book of Allah, Exalted is He, nor more learned than you, nor than your father, nor than your grandfather.' He said: 'Then I testify by Allah that he is the Prophet whom you find in the Torah and the Gospel.' They said: 'You have lied.' Then they turned back against him and said evil things. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood up, and I and Ibn Salam stood up with him. Then Allah sent down: ﴿Say: "Have you considered, if it is from Allah, and you disbelieve in it, and a witness from the Children of Israel testified"﴾, the verse."

A report of his testimony and belief has also been narrated in another way, and the reconciling of it with what has been mentioned does not appear to me. It is also apparent that the descent was after the testimony.

Abd ibn Humayd reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "Maymun ibn Yamin came to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he was the head of the Jews in Medina, and he embraced Islam and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, send to them, that is the Jews, and make between you and them an arbitrator from among themselves, for they will accept me.' So the Prophet (ﷺ) sent to them, and the one who brings guests in brought him in. They came to him and conversed with him at length. He said to them: 'Choose a man from among yourselves who will be an arbitrator between me and you.' They said: 'Indeed we are content with Maymun ibn Yamin.' So he brought him out to them. Maymun said to them: 'We testify that he is the Messenger of Allah, and that he is upon the truth.' But they refused to accept him as truthful. So Allah sent down concerning him: ﴿Say: "Have you considered"﴾, the verse."

This is apparent in the Medinan character of the verse, and that its descent was before the testimony of the witness. However, it is apparent that the witness was not Abdullah ibn Salam. As for whether he was called by that name before, I have not seen it, and the reason for expressing it by that rather than by the one testified about does not appear to me, if there was one. What I have seen in *al-Istiab* in the biography of Abdullah is that he is the son of Salam ibn al-Harith al-Isra'ili al-Ansari, known as Abu Yusuf. His name in the pre-Islamic period was al-Husayn, and when he embraced Islam, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) named him Abdullah. And Allah knows best.

Among the lies and ignorance of the Jews regarding history is what they believe about Abdullah ibn Salam: that when the Prophet (ﷺ) traveled to Syria on a trade mission for Khadijah, may Allah be pleased with her, he met the rabbis of the Jews and related to them his dreams, and they knew that he was a man destined for dominion. So they took Abdullah ibn Salam to accompany him, and he remained with him for a period, and learned from him the knowledge of the laws and of the earlier nations. They exceeded in lying to the point that they attributed the inimitable Qur'an to the composition of Abdullah ibn Salam. This Abdullah had no residence in Mecca, nor any frequenting of it, and he did not see the Prophet (ﷺ) except in Medina, and he embraced Islam when he came to it, peace be upon him, or two years before his death, peace and blessings be upon him, according to what al-Bahr has related from al-Sha'bi. How much the Jews lied and were brazen, may Allah curse them! And consider a group the like of which the Qur'an has never censured.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Masruq that the witness is Musa ibn Imran, peace be upon him. It has already been mentioned that Masruq claimed the verse was Meccan, and denied its descent concerning Ibn Salam, and said: "It was only a dispute which Muhammad (ﷺ) pursued." Apparently, on this view, one does not need to say that it was sent down concerning a particular witness. The non-intention of a particular witness is supported by the argument that ﴿a witness﴾ in the verse is indefinite, and an indefinite in the context of a condition is general. I say: the tanwin of ﴿a witness﴾ is for glorification, and the verse is Medinan, and it was sent down concerning Ibn Salam, and its addresses are in general to the disbelievers of Mecca. It may be assumed in some reports that they are addressed to the Jews, but this is not so. They are also intended by "those who disbelieved" in His words, Exalted is He:

﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾ to the end. This is a report of some other of their false statements concerning the Mighty Qur'an and the believers in it. It also confirms their arrogance. That is, the Meccan disbelievers said ﴿to those who believed﴾, that is, about them and concerning them. Here the lam is for causation (ta'lil), as you have heard in ﴿those who disbelieved said of the truth﴾.

It is also said that the lam is the lam of direct address and conveying (al-mushafahah wal-tabligh), and that the speech turned (iltifat) in their saying ﴿if it had been﴾, meaning what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brought of the Qur'an. It is also said that it refers to faith: ﴿good, they would not have preceded us to it﴾. Had it not been so, they would have said: "You preceded us in the address." Or, having heard that a group had believed, they addressed another group of believers, meaning they said to those who believed: "If it had been good, those (people) whose faith has reached us would not have preceded us to it."

This has been criticised: this is not one of the places of iltifat, and the claim that they intended to belittle the believers by using the third person has no basis. Also, that the ones addressing were a group of the believers and the ones spoken of were another group is contrary to the apparent meaning. So the better view is that the lam is for causation, and they said that because they saw that most of the believers were poor and weak, such as Ammar, Suhayb and Bilal. They used to claim that religious good follows worldly good, and that one is not qualified for the former unless one has the highest share of the latter. For this reason they said: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two towns?﴾ Their error in this is not hidden.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Awn ibn Abi Shaddad, who said: Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) had a slave-woman who had embraced Islam before him, called Zanira, and he (may Allah be pleased with him) used to beat her for her Islam. The disbelievers of Quraysh would say: "If it had been good, Zanira would not have preceded us to it." So Allah sent down concerning her ﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾, the verse. Perhaps they did not intend Zanira specifically, but anyone resembling her as well.

In the verse there is the precedence of the masculine over the feminine (taghlib al-mudhakkar 'ala al-mu'annath). Abu al-Mutawakkil said: Abu Dhar embraced Islam, then the tribe of Ghifar embraced Islam, and Quraysh said that. Al-Kalbi and al-Zajjaj said: Banu Amir ibn Sa'sa'ah, Ghatafan, Asad and Ash'ar said that when Aslam, Juhaynah, Muzaynah and Ghifar embraced Islam. Al-Tha'labi said: it is the saying of the Jews when Ibn Salam and his companions from among them embraced Islam. This would entail that the verse is Medinan, and he counted it among the exceptions. Or (it would be said) that the word ﴿qala﴾ in it is like ﴿nada﴾ in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and the people of the heights will call out﴾. This, as you see, is not satisfactory. What is relied upon is what preceded.

﴿And when they were not guided by it﴾, that is, by the Qur'an. It is also said: by the Messenger (ﷺ). The word ﴿idh﴾ (when), according to what Jar Allah (al-Zamakhshari) chose, is an adverb (zarf) governed by an implied element indicated by what precedes and what follows. That is: "And when they were not guided by it, their obstinacy and arrogance appeared." His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So they will say: this is an ancient falsehood﴾ means that this saying and this slander will occur from them time after time, as the form of the present tense indicates. It is a consequence of obstinacy and arrogance. If something like ﴿hinā'idh﴾ (then) can be used for ﴿al-ān﴾ (now), meaning that this occurred at that time, and "listen now" by the evidence of the context, then this is more permissible. The reference is to the Mighty Qur'an, and their saying "this" about it is like their saying ﴿tales of the ancients﴾. It was not permitted that ﴿fa-sa-yaqulūna﴾ (so they will say) should govern the adverb, because the two indications of past and future conflict. He did not make it like ﴿fa-sawfa ya'lamūn﴾ (so they will come to know) or ﴿idhi al-aghlālu﴾ (when the shackles), placing the future within the sequence of the completed, as Ibn al-Hajib chose in al-Amali. This is because the meaning here, as in al-Kashf, is that the non-guidance is established and has occurred, not that it will definitely occur. Do you not see His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And those who disbelieved said to those who believed﴾, after He had shown their arrogance and obstinacy, how He specifies that they are disputers who turn away from the Qur'an and its contemplation, not guided by its good tidings and warnings?

﴿And before it﴾, that is, before the Qur'an. It is the predicate (khabar) placed before its subject, ﴿the Book of Musa (Moses)﴾, and it was fronted for emphasis (li'l-ihtimam). Al-Tabarsi permitted that ﴿Book﴾ (kitab) be conjoined to ﴿a witness﴾ (shahid), with the adverbial phrase intervening between the conjunction and what is conjoined. The meaning would then be: "and the Book of Musa bore witness before it." He also allowed the pronoun in ﴿before it﴾ to refer to the Qur'an, but this is not valid at all. His statement, ﴿as a leader and a mercy﴾, is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating either to the pronoun in the predicate or to ﴿Book﴾, according to those who permit a circumstantial clause from the subject. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause relating to an omitted noun, with the governing element being the same, meaning "We sent it down as a leader." But this, as you see, is weak.

The meaning is: "Before it there existed the Book of Musa, which was followed in the religion of God, the Exalted, and His laws, just as a leader is followed, and a mercy from God, glorified is He, for whoever believed in it and acted upon its requirements." His statement, the Exalted, ﴿and this﴾, that is, the Qur'an, about which they say what they say, ﴿is a Book﴾, is the subject of a predicate. His statement, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿confirming﴾, is an attribute (na't) of ﴿Book﴾, and it is the locus of the benefit: it confirms the Book of Musa, which is a leader and a mercy, or it confirms what lies between its hands of all the divine Books. It has been read as ﴿confirming what lies between its hands﴾. The sentence is coordinated with the sentence before it, and it is either a circumstantial sentence or a resumed sentence (mustanfa'a). In either case, the discourse is a rejection of their statement, ﴿this is an ancient lie﴾, and a refutation of it. The meaning is: how can it be valid that it is an ancient lie, when they have accepted the Book of Musa, and the Qur'an confirms it and is identical with it in meaning, or confirms all the divine Books? His statement, the Exalted, ﴿in Arabic tongue﴾, is a circumstantial clause relating either to the pronoun of ﴿Book﴾ concealed in ﴿confirming﴾, or to itself, since it is specified by the attribute. Its governing element, according to the first view, is ﴿confirming﴾, and according to the second, it is what this contains of the meaning of a verb. The benefit of this circumstantial clause, although its Arabic character is a matter known to everyone, is to indicate that its being confirming shows, just as it shows that it is true, that it is a revelation and a directive from God, the Exalted.

This applies on the view that the discourse is addressed to the Jews. As for the view that it is addressed to the disbelievers of Makkah, it is because they may accept the Torah and similar divine Books that preceded it, even though at times they deny that Books were sent down and that Messengers, upon them be peace, were sent at all. In the Kashf (al-Kashshaf of al-Zamakhshari), the reason for fronting the predicate in His statement, the Exalted, ﴿And before it the Book of Musa﴾, is that the sending of Messengers and the sending down of Books is a continuous matter from God, the Exalted. Thus, before the sending down of the Qur'an as a leader and a mercy, the sending down of the Torah was likewise. It is not a fronting for exclusivity, but rather because the care and concern lie in mentioning it. When He obliged the disbelievers to produce something similar, and to accept the testimony of the most knowledgeable of the Children of Israel, He mentioned, by way of parenthetical insertion, from the state of the Book of Musa, upon him be peace, what confirms that it is from God, the Exalted, and that what agrees with it must necessarily be from Him, glorified is He. From this He arrives at the conclusion that, since the Qur'an confirms it, indeed confirms all the heavenly Books, it is obligatory to believe in it and receive it with acceptance. This is in reality a restatement of the first claim in a shorter and more comprehensive form, since it indicates that its being confirming is sufficient, whether the witness of the Children of Israel testifies or not. And if it is said that they, because of their obstinacy, were treated as one who does not know that the Book of Musa came before it, since had they known, and it had become clear that it is like it, they would have submitted, then it is said: ﴿and before it﴾, not ﴿after it﴾, would be a fully satisfactory expression in which the right of exclusivity is fulfilled, as al-Sakkaki preferred, namely that it is a necessary consequence of fronting. End. And this is clear in indicating that the sentence is not circumstantial.

The statement would then be by way of an omitted modifier, meaning "possessor of an Arabic tongue," and this refers to the Prophet, upon him be peace and blessings. It is also permitted, on the view of it being an object, that ﴿this﴾ refers to the Book of Musa, so that no omitted modifier is needed. ﴿In Arabic tongue﴾ would then mean the Qur'an, and the demonstrative has been placed in the position of the pronoun for glorification.
