It is explained on the basis that ﴿whoever﴾ (man) is a relative pronoun governed by an omitted verb, and likewise ﴿Book﴾, meaning "and We gave those who were before the descent of the Qur'an among the Children of Israel the Book of Musa."

﴿To warn those who did wrong﴾ is related to ﴿confirming﴾. Within it there is a pronoun referring either to the Book, to God, the Exalted, or to the Messenger, upon him be peace and blessings. The last view is supported by the reading of Abu Raja', Shayba, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Ibn 'Amir, Nafi' and Ibn Kathir, in one transmission, as ﴿to warn﴾ (litunthira) with the second-person ta', because that cannot be applied to anyone other than the Messenger without strain. The causal clause is sound on all readings. There is no concern that the preposition lam would have to be dropped on the view that the pronoun refers to the Book, since the condition for the accusative is present, for that is a condition of permissibility. ﴿And good news for the doers of good﴾ is coordinated with the verbal noun formed from "an" and the verb. Al-Zamakhshari, and Abu al-Baqa' following him, said that it is in the place of the accusative, coordinated with the place of ﴿to warn﴾ (liyunthira), since it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu). Abu Hayyan claimed that this is not permissible according to the sound position of the grammarians, because the place (mahall) is not the original status, and they require for conjoining to it that condition, since the original form of the object of purpose is the genitive, and the accusative arises from the removal of the preposition, though this has become common under its condition. He recounted several possibilities for its i'rab (grammatical analysis). He said: it has been said to be conjoined to ﴿confirming﴾; it has been said to be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "it is good news"; it has been said to be in the accusative by an omitted verb conjoined to (yunthira), meaning "and let him bring good news, good news"; and it has been said to be in the accusative by removal of the preposition, meaning "and for good news." The apparent sense is that ﴿the doers of good﴾ stands in contrast to ﴿those who did wrong﴾. The first refers to the disbelievers, and the second to the believers. In al-Tibi's commentary: he only turned from ﴿the just﴾ to ﴿the doers of good﴾ so that it would be a means toward the good news of the removal of fear and grief for those who said "Our Lord is God" and then went straight. It has been said: "the doers of good" rather than "those who did good" after His statement, the Exalted, ﴿those who did wrong﴾, so that the meaning would be: to warn those in whom wrong was found, and to give good news to those who remained firm and kept to the straight path, which fits the justification of the good news by His statement, the Exalted:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 46, verse 13:

﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast...﴾ up to its end. That is: indeed, those who combine tawhid (monotheism), which is the essence of knowledge (ʿilm), and istiqamah (steadfastness) in the religion, which is the goal of action. ("Thumma," then) denotes a delay in rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), so action is delayed in rank relative to tawhid. The scholars have explicitly stated that action is not considered valid without it. ﴿So no fear will there be upon them﴾ of the onset of something disliked, ﴿nor will they grieve﴾ over the loss of something loved. What is meant is the continuation of the negation. The fa' (in fa-la) is there because the noun contains the meaning of a conditional, while the meaning of the inchoative (ibtida') remains, so it does not enter the predicate of laysa, laʿalla, or kana, even though their nouns are relative pronouns (mawsulat). A parallel to this verse occurred earlier in Surat al-Sajdah, and I explained there what I have explained here, so let it be consulted.

﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ refers to those described by the two sublime attributes mentioned above, ﴿أصْحابُ الجَنَّةِ خالِدِينَ فِيها﴾ ("the companions of the Garden, abiding therein forever"). The phrase ﴿خالِدِينَ فِيها﴾ is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause, describing a state) relating to the hidden pronoun (al-mustakinn) in أصْحابُ. As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿جَزاءً﴾, it is manṣūb (in the accusative case), either by a governing verb (ʿāmil) that is implied, meaning "they will be recompensed with a recompense," in which case the sentence is either an independent resumptive clause (istiʾnāf, a new sentence that begins a fresh point) or a ḥāl. Or it is accusative by the sense of what came before, as it has been said: His saying, ﴿أُولَئِكَ أصْحابُ الجَنَّةِ﴾, carries the meaning "We have recompensed them" (jāzaynāhum). And ﴿بِما كانُوا يَعْمَلُونَ﴾ means "for what they used to do," namely the good deeds, both those of the heart and those of the body.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 46, verse 15 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents.﴾ It was revealed, as Ibn 'Asakir narrated through al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him),
[p. 17]
up to His words, ﴿the true promise which they were promised.﴾

(*Ihsanan*) [kindness]: It is said to be a second object of *wassayna* (We enjoined), on the principle of *tadmin* (implicit meaning, where a verb is given the sense of another verb to which it is connected), with the sense of *alzamna* (We obligated). It is also said to be an accusative of the verbal noun (*masdar*), with *wassayna* implicitly carrying the sense of *ahsanna* (We did good), meaning: We did good by enjoining upon man, concerning his parents, kindness. It is also said to be an adjective of a deleted verbal noun, with an elided genitive construction, meaning: an enjoining that is kind. It is also said to be an object of purpose, meaning: We enjoined him concerning them because of Our kindness to them. Ibn 'Atiyya said that it is an accusative of the pure verbal noun. (*Bi-walidayhi*) [concerning his parents] is connected to *wassayna*, or to *ihsanan*. It seems that he meant: "He does good, a kindness," and this is good. However, Abu Hayyan objected to the permission of connecting the prepositional phrase to *ihsanan*, saying that it is not valid, because it is a verbal noun estimated to be with a verbal-noun particle and a verb, and so its complement may not precede it. Also, *ahsana* is not transitive with *bi* (with); it is transitive with *li* (to). One says *ahsantu li-Zayd* (I did good to Zayd), not *ahsantu bi-Zayd*, in the sense that the kindness reaches him. Yet we do not grant that what is estimated by something shares all the rulings of what it is estimated by, since it is possible that some of its rulings are specific to its explicit wording. Moreover, the adverbial phrase is sufficient with the faint trace of the verb, which is why a rigid noun works in it by considering the verbal-noun meaning. Some said: it receives treatment that other things do not receive, because most things need it.

The prepositional phrase and its object are treated as dependent on it. There are many instances where it seems to be connected to a verbal noun that comes later, whether indefinite, as in ﴿and let not pity for them take hold of you﴾, or definite, as in ﴿and when he reached with him the effort﴾. Interpreting all of that is artificial. Also, his statement "because *ahsana* is not transitive with *bi*," and so on, contains a clear objection. Some scholars estimated the verb before the prepositional phrase and said: "We enjoined man to be good to his parents, a great goodness." It may be that the tanwin (nunation) is for magnification, meaning great kindness. *Al-iya'* (enjoining) and *al-wasiyya* (the charge) mean to put forward to another what he should act upon, together with admonition, from the expression *ard wasiya* (land whose plants are interconnected). The verse thus indicates that kindness to them is a matter of special concern. In a hadith it is counted as the second-best of deeds, which is prayer at its earliest time, and disobedience to them is counted as the second-greatest of major sins, which is associating partners with Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The hadiths encouraging the first and warning against the second are very numerous, and in the verses there is sufficiency for one who gives ear while he is a witness.

Al-Jumhur (the majority) read *husnan* with a *damma* on the *ha'* and a sukun on the *sin*, meaning a deed possessing goodness, or as though it is in itself the very essence of goodness due to its extreme goodness. Abu Hayyan permitted that it could have the sense of *ihsanan*, so the preceding opinions apply to it. Ali (may Allah ennoble his face), al-Sulami, and 'Isa read *hasanan* with a fatha on the *ha'* and the *sin*. It is reported from 'Isa that he read *husunan* with a damma on both.

﴿His mother bore him with hardship, and she gave birth to him with hardship.﴾ That is, in a state of hardship, or a pregnancy accompanied by hardship, which is difficulty, as Mujahid, al-Hasan, and Qatadah said. The hardship is not at the beginning of conception, but after that, when she finds a heaviness in him. Shaybah, Abu Ja'far, and the two men of Mecca and Medina (*al-Haramayn*) read *karhan* with a fatha on the *kaf*. They are two dialects with the same meaning, like *al-faqr* and *al-fuqr*, and *al-di'f* and *al-du'f*. It is also said that the damma-form is a noun and the fatha-form is a verbal noun.

Al-Raghib said: It is said that *al-karh* with a fatha is the hardship that befalls a person from outside, from what is forced upon him by compulsion, while *al-kurh* with a damma is what befalls him from within himself, which is what he dislikes in terms of nature, or in terms of reason or sharia. Abu Hatim criticized this reading, saying: "This reading is not good, because *al-karh* with a fatha means compulsion and domination." You know that it is among the seven mutawatir readings, so there is no sense in criticizing it. This man used to criticize some readings with what he had no knowledge of, out of audacity. May Allah pardon him.

﴿And his carrying and his weaning﴾ means the period of his carrying and his weaning. By estimating this genitive construction, the statement of Allah, ﴿thirty months,﴾ can be taken as the predicate of the subject without hardship.

*Al-fisal* (weaning) is weaning, and it is a verbal noun of the form *fa'al*, so it is as if the child separates his mother and she separates him. Abu Raja', al-Hasan, Qatadah, Ya'qub, and al-Jahdari read *wa-fasluhu* (and his separation), meaning his weaning. So *al-fasl* and *al-fisal* are like *al-fatm* and *al-fitam* in form and meaning. It is also said that *al-fisal* has the meaning of the time of separation, that is, of weaning, so it is conjoined to the period of carrying. The intended meaning of *al-fisal* is complete nursing that ends with weaning, and for this reason it expresses it, or its time, rather than general nursing, for that does not convey this. The description is lengthy. The verse is an explanation of what the mother endures and suffers in raising the child, an exaggeration in enjoining her. For this reason the Lawgiver (*al-shari'*) gave special attention to her kindness above attention to kindness to the father. It was narrated that a man said: "O Messenger of Allah, who is most deserving of my kindness?" He said: "Your mother." He said: "Then who?" He said: "Your mother." He said: "Then who?" He said: "Your mother." He said: "Then who?" He said: "Your father."

The verse has alluded to what requires kindness to her in particular, in three levels, so the commands in the report are as if derived from that. 'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face), Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them), and a group of scholars took it as evidence that the minimum period of pregnancy is six months, because when thirty months is reduced by the two years of weaning (based on His words, ﴿two full years for whoever wishes to complete the nursing﴾), six months remain for the pregnancy. The physicians also said so. Galen said: "I was keen in investigating the duration of pregnancy, and I saw a woman who gave birth after one hundred and eighty-four nights." Ibn Sina claimed that he had witnessed this.

As for the maximum period of pregnancy, there is nothing in the Noble Qur'an that indicates it. Ibn Sina said in *al-Shifa'*: "It reached me from someone I completely trust that a woman gave birth after the fourth year of pregnancy to a child whose teeth had grown." It is reported from Aristotle that he said: "The periods of pregnancy for every animal are fixed, except for humans. A woman may give birth at seven months, and may give birth at eight, and rarely does a child survive in the eighth month except in certain lands, such as Egypt." Perhaps the specification of the minimum pregnancy and the maximum nursing in the Noble Qur'an by explicit statement and indication, rather than the maximum pregnancy and the minimum nursing and the average of both, is because these are fixed by not being subject to decrease or increase, unlike what was mentioned. The link between the ruling of lineage and the minimum period of pregnancy is established: if she gives birth within less than it, his lineage is not established from him, but after it, it is established, and the child is cleared of illegitimacy. If a wet nurse nurses after two years, the rulings of nursing are not established through it in matters of marriage and other things. There is a disagreement on this that is not regarded.

﴿Until, when he reaches his maturity﴾ is an endpoint for an estimated clause, meaning: he lived, or his life continued, until, when he reached full strength, his power and his intellect became firm. ﴿And reaches forty years﴾ The apparent meaning is that it is other than reaching maturity. Some said that it is the reaching of maturity, and the conjunction is for emphasis.

Many have mentioned that when a person reaches this measure, his character, which he has, becomes very strong, so he hardly ever departs from it afterwards. In a hadith: "Indeed, Satan drags his hand over the face of whoever exceeds forty and does not repent, and says: 'By my father, a face that will not prosper!'" Abu al-Fath al-Azdi narrated through Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, as a raised report (*marfu'*): "Whoever reaches forty years and his good does not outweigh his evil, let him prepare himself for the Fire."

Upon this is the saying of the poet:
When a man reaches forty and has no shame or veil beyond what he desires,
Then leave him, and do not grudge him what has passed, even if life's causes have drawn out his lifetime for him.

It is said: No prophet was sent except after forty. Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) went against this, arguing that 'Isa and Yahya (peace be upon them both) were sent as boys, based on the apparent meaning of what is reported about them in the Glorious Book. This is also the apparent meaning of the words of al-Sa'd (al-Taftazani), where he said: "Among the conditions of prophethood are being male, full intellect, intelligence, understanding, and strength of judgment, even in youth, like 'Isa and Yahya (peace be upon them both)," and so on to the end of what he said.

Ibn al-'Arabi and others went to the view that it is permissible for Allah, Glorified be He, to send a boy as a prophet, but that it did not happen. They interpreted the two verses about 'Isa and Yahya, ﴿He said: Indeed I am the servant of Allah; He has given me the Book and made me a prophet.﴾

﴿And We gave him judgment as a boy﴾ — they explained that these are reports about what would be attained by both of them,
[p. 19]
not about what had already occurred. Its like is frequent in the verses and elsewhere. What occurs according to these scholars is that the sending as a prophet happens after maturity. Al-Laqqani reported from some that he stipulated maturity for it. My own view is that it is more likely that maturity is stipulated for it, but not for the essence of prophethood, because souls in most cases recoil from following a young person, even if he is greatly superior, just as they do with a slave and a female. A group explicitly stated that the more general and more common case is that the sending occurs at the age of forty, as happened with our Prophet (ﷺ).

﴿He said: My Lord, inspire me﴾, that is: encourage me and enable me, from *awza'tuhu bi-kadha*, meaning I made him attached to it, eager to attain it. Al-Bazzi read *awza'ni* with a fatha on the *ya'* (*awza'niya*). ﴿That I may thank Your favor which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents﴾, that is, the favor of religion, or what includes it and other things. This supports what is narrated, that it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him), because no one among the Muhajirun (emigrants) and the Ansar (helpers) had embraced Islam, he and his parents together, except him, so it is said. But his father embraced Islam after the conquest, and then it would follow that the verse is Medinan, and some scholars went to this. It was said: this supplication with regard to his parents is a supplication for their guidance to faith, and this, as you see, is weak. The reasoning was objected to with Ibn 'Umar, Usama ibn Zayd, and others. It is reported from al-Wahidi that he accompanied the Prophet (ﷺ) when he was eighteen years old, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was twenty years old, on a trade journey to Syria. He rested under a sidr tree, and the monk said to him: "No one has sat under it after 'Isa except him (ﷺ)." So belief in his word entered his heart, and he did not leave him in travel or at home. When he was made a prophet at forty, he believed in him at thirty-eight. When he reached forty, he said: ﴿My Lord, inspire me,﴾ etc.

﴿And that I may do righteous deeds that You approve﴾. The tanwin is for magnification and amplification. What is meant by His being pleased with it, though pleasure, according to the majority of the people of truth, is will together with non-objection, is that every righteous deed of this kind must be free from the pitfalls of non-acceptance, such as showing off, self-admiration, and other things. Its summary is: make my deeds conform to Your pleasure. It was also said that what is meant by pleasure here is its fruit, by way of metonymy (*kinaya*). ﴿And set right for me my offspring﴾, that is: make righteousness spread among my descendants and firmly established in them, as in the saying:
If you apologize in the place, from among her udders,
In the place where my blade is cutting her hamstrings.

On the basis that (أَصْلِحْ) (*aṣliḥ*, "make righteous") was used in the intransitive sense (*manzilat al-lāzim*), and was then made transitive with (فِي) (*fī*, "in") to convey what we have pointed to: the goodness spreads among them, and they are like a container for it, because it is firmly settled in them. Otherwise the expected form would have been (وَأَصْلِحْ لِي ذُرِّيَّتِي) (*wa-aṣliḥ lī dhurriyyatī*, "and make my offspring righteous for me"). It has also been said that (فِي) (*fī*) was used because the verb includes the meaning of kindness, that is, "Be kind to me regarding my offspring." The first view is better.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: Allah the Exalted answered the supplication of Abu Bakr. He freed nine believers, among them Bilal and ʿAmir ibn Fuhayrah, and he did not intend any good except that Allah the Exalted helped him to it. He also supplicated, saying (أَصْلِحْ لِي فِي ذُرِّيَّتِي) (*aṣliḥ lī fī dhurriyyatī*, "make my offspring righteous for me"), and Allah the Exalted answered him, so that none of his children remained except that they all believed. Thus the Islam of both his parents and all his children was gathered for him. His father, and his son ʿAbd al-Rahman, and his son's son Abu ʿAtiq, met the Prophet (ﷺ) and believed in him. This did not happen to anyone else among the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all.

﴿إِنِّي تُبْتُ إِلَيْكَ﴾ (*Indeed, I have turned to You in repentance*) from what You do not approve of, or what distracts from You.

﴿وَإِنِّي مِنَ الْمُسْلِمِينَ﴾ (*And indeed, I am among the Muslims*), those who have sincerely devoted themselves to You.

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to mankind (al-insan), and the plural is used because what is meant is the category (jins) characterized by the meaning mentioned. The sense of distance in it serves to indicate the remoteness of their station and the loftiness of their rank. That is, "those who are described by the noble attributes mentioned."

﴿from whom We accept the best of what they did﴾ of acts of obedience, for a permissible act (mubah) is good but is not rewarded for. ﴿and We overlook their evil deeds﴾ because of their repentance, which is indicated by "I have repented." Otherwise, according to the People of Truth (Ahl al-Haqq), forgiveness of sin in general is not contingent upon repentance ﴿among the companions of the Garden﴾

[Page 20]

Being among their number, enrolled in their row. It has been said that "fi" (in) here means "ma'a" (with), but this is not the correct view. ﴿a true promise﴾ is a verbal noun (masdar) for a verb that is implied, and it emphasizes the content of the sentence before it, for His statement, glorified is He, "We accept and We overlook," is a promise from Him, mighty and majestic, of acceptance and overlooking.

﴿which they were promised﴾ upon the tongues of the Messengers, peace be upon them. It was also read as (yutaqabbalu) with the letter ya' and in the passive voice, with (ahsanu) in the nominative as a substitute for the subject (nai'b al-fa'il), and likewise (yatajawwazu 'an sayyi'atihim).

And al-Hasan, al-A'mash and 'Isa read both with the letter ya' in the active voice, the subject being His pronoun, exalted is His majesty, and (ahsana) in the accusative as the object.

﴿And he who says to his two parents﴾ when they call him to faith, ﴿"Uff to you both!"﴾ *Uff* is a sound that issues from a person when he is annoyed. It has about forty readings and dialects (*qira'at* and *lughat*, the recognized Qur'anic readings and the variant forms of pronunciation). We have drawn attention to this in Surat al-Isra'. The *lam* in ﴿لَكُما﴾ indicates the one for whom the exclamation is uttered, as in ﴿Hayta laka﴾ ("Come, I am yours"). The relative pronoun ﴿الَّذِي﴾ is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is ﴿أُولَئِكَ الَّذِينَ حَقَّ عَلَيْهِمُ الْقَوْلُ﴾ ("those are the ones against whom the Word has been justly fulfilled"). The intended meaning is the category, so it has the sense of the plural, which is why ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ ("those") is used. Al-Hasan indicated this when he said: "He is the disbelieving son who is undutiful to his parents and who denies the Resurrection." The revelation of the verse about a particular person does not preclude its generality, as has been established more than once. Marwan claimed, may he deserve what he deserves, that it was revealed about Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with them both), and Aishah (may Allah be pleased with her) refuted him.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abdullah, who said: "I was in the mosque when Marwan delivered a sermon and said: 'Indeed Allah has shown the Commander of the Faithful, meaning Mu'awiya, a good opinion regarding Yazid, that he should appoint him as successor, for Abu Bakr and Umar appointed successors.' Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr said: 'Heraclian! By Allah, Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) did not make it [the caliphate] for any of his sons or any of the members of his household, and Mu'awiya did not make it except as mercy and honour for his son.' Marwan said: 'Are you not the one who said to his parents, "Uff to you both!"?' Abd al-Rahman said: 'Are you not the son of the accursed whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cursed, your father?' Aishah heard this and said: 'Marwan, you are the one who said such and such about Abd al-Rahman. You are lying. By Allah, it was not revealed about him. It was revealed about so-and-so, son of so-and-so.'"

In another report, mentioned earlier, narrated by a group and authenticated by al-Hakim, from Muhammad ibn Ziyad, she denied his claim three times and then said: "By Allah, he is not the one meant," meaning her brother. "If I wished to name the one about whom it was revealed, I would name him," and so on as mentioned above. This was a remnant of the curse, intended to enrage Abd al-Rahman and to turn people away from him, so that they would not heed what he said. Yet he spoke only the truth. Where is Yazid, whom the curse should be far above, and where is the caliphate?

Some scholars, such as al-Suhayli in *al-I'lam*, agreed with Marwan that it was revealed about Abd al-Rahman. Even if this is granted, there is no sense in reproach, especially from Marwan, for this man had embraced Islam, was one of the eminent Companions and their heroes, and had a notable role in Islam at the Battle of Yamama and elsewhere. Islam erases what came before it. Thus, when a disbeliever embraces Islam, he should not be reproached for what he used to say.

﴿"Do you promise me that I will be brought forth?"﴾ that I will be raised from the grave after death. Al-Hasan, Asim, Abu Amr in one narration, and Hisham read ﴿أتَعِدانِّي﴾ with idgham (assimilation) of the nun of the raising case (*nun al-rafʿ*) into the protective nun (*nun al-wiqaya*). Nafi' in one narration and a group read it with one nun. Al-Hasan, Shayba, Abu Ja'far (in a variant report from him), Abd al-Warith from Abu Amr, Harun ibn Musa from al-Jahdari, and Bassam from Hisham read ﴿أتِعَدانَنِي﴾ with two nuns without idgham, and with the first nun vocalized with a fatha. It seems they fled from the juxtaposition of two kasras and the *ya'*, so they used the fatha for lightness. Abu Hatim said: "Fathah on the nun is false and an error." Some said: "The fathah on the nun of the dual is a poor dialect." Here, however, the juncture of the sounds eases the matter.

Al-Hasan, Ibn Ya'mur, al-A'mash, Ibn Musarrif, and al-Dahhak read ﴿أخْرَجَ﴾ in the active voice, from *al-khurūj* (going out). ﴿"And generations have passed away before me"﴾ that is, they have passed on, and none of them came out or was raised. Thus the intent is the denial of the Resurrection, as has been said:

*No one has come to us to tell us that he is in a Garden or a Fire for those who have passed.*

Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: "He meant: 'And generations have passed away before me, denying the Resurrection.' So the statement is like an argument for the negation of the Resurrection."

﴿And they both call upon Allah for help﴾ that is, they say: "Help is from Allah against you." The intent is to deny his statement and to magnify it, as if they had sought refuge in Allah, glorified is He, to repel it, as one says: "We seek refuge in Allah from such and such." Or they seek from Allah, mighty and majestic, that He help him with success until he returns from his denial of the Resurrection. ﴿"Woe to you! Believe!"﴾ that is, saying this to him, or they say it to him. The origin of *waylun* (woe) is a supplication for destruction, used in place of urging the doing or abandoning of an act, indicating that what one is engaged in is deserving of the ruin of its doer, and that destruction should be sought for him. When he hears this, it prompts him to abandon what he is in and to take hold of what saves him. It has been said that this is because it implies that the act he is commanded to do is something to be envied, so destruction is invoked upon him, and when he hears this he desires it. Whatever the case, the intent here is exhortation and encouragement to faith, not the literal supplication for destruction. ﴿"Indeed, the promise of Allah is true"﴾ that is, the Resurrection. He attributed the promise to Allah, exalted is He, to affirm the truth and to alert him to his error in attributing the promise to them. Al-A'raj and Amr ibn Fa'id read ﴿أنَّ﴾ with a fatha on the hamza, on the basis of *li-anna* (because) or *āmanu bi-anna* (believe that). The first reading is preferred because it harmonizes the two readings.

﴿Then he says﴾ denying them both: "What is this that you call the promise of Allah? ﴿It is nothing but the fables of the ancients﴾ their falsehoods which they inscribed in books, with no reality behind them."

صفحة 21

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 46, verse 18:

﴿Ulā'ika﴾ (Those) are the ones saying that. It is also said: that is, the category of this one mentioned, based on the claim that it refers specifically to ﴿alladhī﴾ (the one [singular]). But this is not valid.

﴿Alladhīna ḥaqqa ʿalayhimu al-qawl﴾ (Those against whom the word has come into effect), which is His saying, exalted is He, to Iblis: ﴿"I will surely fill Hell with you and with those among them who follow you, all together."﴾ The full discussion of this has already passed. By this, a refutation is made against the one who claimed that the verse refers to ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr, because he, may Allah be pleased with him, embraced Islam, and what was before it was erased from him, and he was among the eminent Companions. And the one against whom the word has come into effect is the one whom Allah knows will never believe. It is also said: the judgment here is upon the kind (genus), so it does not contradict the exclusion of some of them from its otherworldly rulings. And other things have been said which are not worth attention.

﴿Fī umamin qad khalat min qablihim﴾ (among nations that had passed away before them), in correspondence with ﴿fī aṣḥāb al-jannah﴾ (among the companions of the Garden). So it is similar to it in grammatical analysis (iʿrab), emphasis, and meaning. And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿min al-jinni wa'l-ins﴾ (from among the jinn and mankind), is an explanation of the nations. ﴿Innahum﴾ (Indeed they), all of them, ﴿kānū khāsirīn﴾ (were losers). They wasted their original natural disposition (fitrah), which functions like the capital of their wealth, by following Satan. The sentence is a justification of the ruling by way of resumption (istiʾnaf). Al-ʿAbbas narrated from Abu ʿAmr a reading of (annahum) with the hamzah opened, on the assumption of li-annahum (because they). It has been cited as evidence, by His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿among nations that had passed away﴾, etc., that the jinn die generation after generation just like humans. In al-Bahr it is related that al-Hasan said in some of his gatherings: "The jinn do not die," and Qatadah objected to him with this verse, and he fell silent.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 46, verse 19:

﴿Wa-li-kull﴾ (for each) of the two groups mentioned in His saying, ﴿Those from whom We accept the best of what they did﴾, and in His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Those upon whom the Word has been justified﴾, and if you wish, say: [it refers to] those who said, "Our Lord is Allah," and the one who said to his parents, "Uff!" ﴿are degrees according to what they did﴾, i.e., degrees of the recompense for what they did. The statement is thus elliptical (bi-taqdir mudaf), and the prepositional phrase is an attribute of (darajat, degrees). The (min) is either explanatory (bayaniyyah) or initial (ibtida'iyyah), and (ma) is either relative (mawsulah), meaning "from that which they did of good and evil," or verbal-masdar (masdariyyah), meaning "from their doing of good and evil." It is also permissible for (min) to be causal (ta'lîliyyah) without the elliptical noun and the prepositional phrase, as has been mentioned above.

Darajat is the plural of daraja (degree), which is close in meaning to manzilah (station). However, daraja is used for a station when considered in terms of ascent, and darak when considered in terms of descent. For this reason it is said: "the degrees of Paradise" and "the depths (darakat) of Hellfire."

The expression by "degrees," as many have said, is by way of subordinating the one to the other (taghlib), since (kull, each) includes the two groups. That is, for each there are stations and ranks, whether they are degrees or depths. The people of the degrees predominated because they are most deserving of it, especially since their recompense has been mentioned repeatedly and the recompense of the opposite party only once. ﴿And that He may pay them in full their deeds﴾, i.e., the recompense of their deeds, and the agent is His pronoun, exalted is He. Al-A'mash, al-A'raj, Shaybah, Abu Ja'far, the two brothers (al-Akhawan), Ibn Dhakwan, and Nafi' (with a variant transmitted from him) read (li-nuwaffiya-hum) with the nun of majesty. As-Sulami read with a feminine ta' on the basis of attributing the verb to "degrees" metaphorically. ﴿And they will not be wronged﴾ by a reduction in reward or an increase in punishment. The discussion of similar expressions has passed more than once. The clause is a circumstantial (hal) clause emphasizing the paying in full, or a resumptive statement confirming it. The lam is connected to a deleted element placed later, as if it were said: "and that He may pay them in full their deeds, and not wrong them," in the manner of what was done in fixing the recompenses according to the measures of their deeds, so that reward was made into degrees and punishment into depths.

[Commentary of al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on Surah 46, verse 20]

﴿And on the Day when those who disbelieve are exposed to the Fire﴾: that is, they are tormented by it, from the expression of the Arabs: "The people of so-and-so were exposed to the sword" when they were killed by it. This is a widespread figurative usage (*majaz*). Some scholars held that it is of the type of *al-qalb al-ma'nawi* (semantic inversion, where the sense is reversed in the structure of the sentence), and the meaning is: "On the Day when the Fire is presented to those who disbelieve," similar to the phrase "the she-camel was presented to the watering trough" (*'aradat al-naqatu 'ala al-hawd*). Its meaning is also, as they said, "the watering trough was presented to the she-camel" (*'arada al-hawdu 'ala al-naqah*), because the one to whom something is presented must have perception, so that it may incline toward what is presented or turn away from it. However, since the appropriate arrangement is that the presented thing be brought to the one to whom it is presented and moved toward him, and here the matter is the reverse, because the watering trough was not brought to the camel, and likewise the Fire, the expression has been inverted in observance of this consideration.

In *al-Intisaf* it is said: If the phrase "the she-camel was presented to the watering trough" is inverted, then the words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿and on the Day when those who disbelieve are exposed to the Fire﴾ are not so, because the one compelled there to the belief of the heart is that the watering trough is inanimate and has no perception, while the she-camel is the perceiving one. So it is she to whom the watering trough is presented in reality. As for the Fire, the texts have stated that on that Day it will have perception like the perception of living creatures, indeed like the perception of those possessed of knowledge. So the matter in the verse is on its apparent sense, like your saying: "The captives were presented to the commander." It may be said: There is no obstacle to treating it as if it were perceiving, even if it is not then perceiving, and likewise treating the watering trough as if it were in that position, so that it is as though it were seeking out the she-camel, as Abu al-'Ala al-Ma'arri said:

*When the horses long for the watering places, they turn away from the water, and then the watering places long for them.*

After this, there may be no need to posit semantic inversion. Abu Hayyan said: It is not appropriate to interpret the Qur'an as containing inversion; the correct view is that it is something needed only in poetry. And when the meaning is sound and clear without it, what necessity calls for it? The example mentioned contains no inversion either, for the presenting of the she-camel to the watering trough and the presenting of the watering trough to the she-camel are each correct, since "presenting" is a relational matter whose attribution is valid to each of the she-camel and the watering trough. Ibn al-Sikkit, in *al-Tawsi'ah*, held that "the watering trough was presented to the she-camel" is inverted, and that the original is only "the she-camel was presented to the watering trough," but this contradicts what is well known. You know, from what we mentioned at the beginning, that the reason they posited inversion in the example is that the appropriate form of presenting is that the presented thing be brought to the one to whom it is presented, and that in "the watering trough was presented to the she-camel" the matter is the reverse. The detailed discussion of this, in a way by which the source of the disagreement is known, is that presenting in absolute terms does not require that; what requires it is the intended meaning of presenting in the example, which is inclination toward the presented thing. Whoever does not consider this meaning, but considers that the one presenting moves toward the one to whom it is presented, said that this is the original sense. Whoever considers neither of these two aspects and says that "presenting" means the showing of one thing to another, said that each of the two statements is on the original sense. And, as the scholar al-Salakuti said, the truth is that both aspects lie outside the concept of "presenting," so memorize this, for it is precious.

[Page 23]

The adverbial phrase (*al-zarf*) is governed by an omitted verb whose statement is the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿You used up your good things﴾ to the end of the verse. That is: it will be said to them on the Day when they are exposed, "You used up your pleasures ﴿in your life of the world﴾ by enjoying them ﴿and you took your enjoyment of them﴾, so nothing of them remains for you after this." This is an explanatory conjunction (*'atf tafsir*) for "you used up." Qatadah, Mujahid, Ibn Thabit, Abu Ja'far, al-Hasan, al-A'raj and Ibn Kathir read *a-dhhabtum* with a hamzah followed by a long vowel, and Ibn 'Amir read it with two hamzahs, the first of which Ibn Dhakwan realized and Ibn Hisham softened the second. Ibn Kathir in one narration, and Hisham in another, placed an alif between the realized and the softened hamzah. The interrogative here is in the sense of reproach, so it is in meaning a statement; if it were a pure interrogative, the fa' would not have entered into His words, glorified is He:

﴿So today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation﴾, that is, *al-hawn*, humiliation. Likewise it was read ﴿for what you used to﴾ in the world ﴿be arrogant about in the earth without right﴾, without entitlement to that. The secret of "in the earth" and "for what you used to transgress" has already been explained. That is: you went out from the obedience of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because of your arrogance and your persistent transgression. In *al-Bahr* it is said that arrogance is meant as the rising above faith, and transgression as the sins of the limbs, and the sin of the heart is mentioned before the sins of the limbs, since the deeds of the limbs arise from the will of the heart. It was also read *tafsiqun* with a kasrah on the sin. This verse urges moderation in worldly matters, abandoning luxury in them, and taking up asceticism.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* reported from Ibn 'Umar that 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, saw a dirham in the hand of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him, and said: "What is this dirham?" He said: "I want to buy meat with it for my family, for they craved it." He said: "Whenever you desire something, do you buy it? Where will this verse leave you? ﴿You used up your good things in your life of the world and you took your enjoyment of them﴾."

Ibn al-Mubarak, Ibn Sa'd, Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, 'Abd ibn Humayd, and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilyah* reported from al-Hasan who said: A delegation of the people of Basra came to 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, with Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, and he had bread soaked each day. Sometimes we found it accompanied by oil, sometimes by ghee, sometimes by milk, and sometimes we found dried, pounded meat boiled over it. And sometimes we found fresh meat, which was rare. He said: 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said to us: "By Allah, I am not ignorant of the choice parts of the camel's flank and hump, nor of roasted meat, nor of fried dishes, but I have found that Allah, the Exalted, reproached a people for a deed they did, and He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿You used up your good things in your life of the world and you took your enjoyment of them﴾."

*Al-karakir* is the plural of *kirkirah* (with a kasrah), the chest-pad of the camel which touches the ground when it kneels, and it is one of the finest parts to eat. *Al-asnimah* is the plural of *sanam*, the hump, well known. *Al-sila'* (with a kasrah and a long vowel) means roasted meat. *Al-sinab* (like *kitab*) is a dye made from mustard and raisins. *Al-salA'iq* is the plural of *saliqah* (like *safinah*), what is boiled of herbs and others; it is also narrated with a *sad* as *al-sulaqah*, meaning flat bread, its singular being *saliqah*, also like *safinah*. It was said: it is the roasted lambs, and it was said: roasted meat well cooked. They recited for Jarir:

*He burdens me with the livelihood of the family of Zayd, and who will provide me with the fried dishes and the dyes?*

Ahmad and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* reported from Thawban, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ travelled, his last act with his family was with Fatimah, and the first person who entered upon him from them was Fatimah, may Allah be pleased with her. He returned from a campaign he had made and came to her, and behold, there was a hanging of coarse cloth on her door, and he saw on al-Hasan and al-Husayn two silver bracelets. So he turned back and did not enter upon her. When she saw that, she thought that he had not entered because of what he had seen. So she tore the curtain and removed the two bracelets from the two children and cut them, and they wept. She divided that between them, and they went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while they were weeping. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ took it from them and said: 'O Thawban, take this to the house of so-and-so, the people of a house in Madinah, and buy for Fatimah a necklace of *'asb* and two bracelets of ivory, for these are the people of my household, and I do not like them to consume their good things in their life of the world.'"

*Al-misḥ* (with a kasrah and a sukun) is a garment of thick hair. *Al-qulbayn* is the dual of *qulb* (with a dammah and a sukun), meaning a bracelet. *Al-'asb* (with a fathah and a sukun): al-Khattabi said: "If it is not the Yemeni garments, then I do not know what it is, nor do I know that necklaces are made of it." It may be that the narration is with a *sad*, *al-asbab*, meaning the sinews of the joints of animals, so perhaps they used to make from its pure part something like beads.

He said: Then some of the people of Yemen mentioned that *al-'asb* is the tooth of a sea creature called "Pharaoh's horse," from which white beads and other things are made. The narrations on asceticism concerning the good things of the life of this world are numerous, and the condition of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in this matter is well known among the community. In *al-Bahr*, after relating the condition of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, in a manner similar to what we mentioned, Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: "This is of the type of asceticism; otherwise the verse was revealed concerning the disbelievers of Quraysh, and the meaning is that for you there were good things of the Hereafter had you believed, but you did not believe, so you hastened your good things in the life of this world." This is then a metonymy for the absence of faith, and for this reason the words ﴿So today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation﴾ follow from it. If the literal sense were intended, and it were not a metonymy for what we have mentioned, the recompense of punishment would not follow from it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 46, verse 21:

Now, since the people of Makkah were absorbed in the pleasures of this world and turned away from faith and from what the Messenger (ﷺ) had brought, it was fitting to remind them of what befell the earlier Arabs who had more wealth, greater strength, and higher standing than they did, so that punishment was inflicted upon them because of their disbelief. Through the citing of examples (*darb al-amthal*) and the stories of those who came before, the ugliness and the goodness of things become known. So Allah, glorified is He, said to His Messenger (ﷺ): ﴿And mention﴾ to the disbelievers of Makkah ﴿the brother of 'Ad﴾, Hud (peace be upon him), ﴿when he warned his people﴾. This is a *badal al-ishtimal* (substitution of inclusion) from it, meaning: at the time of his warning them. ﴿In al-Ahqaf﴾: the plural of *hiqf*, a long sand dune that has curvature and bending. It is said *ihqawqafa al-shay'* (the thing became crooked). They were nomadic people, dwellers of tents and pillars, living among sand dunes overlooking the sea, in a land called al-Shajar from the lands of Yemen; this is what Ibn Zayd said. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: between 'Uman and Mahra. In another narration from him: al-Ahqaf is a mountain in al-Sham. Ibn Ishaq said: their dwellings were from 'Uman to Hadramawt. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the correct view is that the land of 'Ad was in Yemen, and Iram *dhat al-'imad* (of the pillars) was theirs. Allah willing, the discussion of Iram and the clarification of the truth concerning it will come later.

﴿And there have passed away warners﴾, i.e., messengers, as is well known. It has been said that it includes all of them and their deputies. *Nudur* is the plural of *nadhir* in the sense of *munzir* (one who warns). It is also permissible that *al-nudur* is the plural of *nadhir* in the sense of *indhar* (warning), in which case it is a verbal noun, and it was made plural because it varies according to what is warned against. It has been objected that its plural form is contrary to analogy, and there is no need for it. ﴿From before him﴾, i.e., from before him (peace be upon him), ﴿and from behind him﴾, i.e., after him. It was also read with this meaning. Were it not so, the reverse would be permissible. The apparent meaning is that the intended warners are those who came before him and those who came after him. From Ibn 'Abbas: he means the messengers who were sent before him and those who were sent during his time. So the meaning of ﴿from behind him﴾ is after his warning. The conjunction of ﴿from behind him﴾, i.e., after him, with what precedes it is either from the type of "I fed her straw and cool water," and there are views on this. It has been said: the second verb is implied, meaning "and I gave her water to drink," and it is said in the verse, meaning: the warners passed away from before him, and will come after him. It has also been said that this is *mushakala* (harmonization of wording), and it has been said that it is of the kind of *al-isti'arah bil-kinayah* (metaphor by implication). Or it is for including the future in the category of the past, with certainty of occurrence, and in this there is a trace of combining literal and figurative meaning. It is also permissible to say: the past tense is with respect to the fixity of the matter in the knowledge of Allah, Exalted is He, meaning: the passing away of the warners, both those who passed and those who will come, was established in His knowledge, glorified is He. The clause may be either a *hal* (circumstantial clause) from the subject of *andhara* (he warned), meaning: when he warned them, informing them of the passing away of the warners, or from its object, meaning: while they were aware through his informing them. This is close to the style of His saying: ﴿How do you disbelieve in Allah when you were dead?﴾ [2:28], the verse. It is also possible that the meaning is that he warned them during a *fatrah* (interval) between messengers, which is also a circumstantial clause according to Ibn 'Abbas's interpretation. The people's knowledge may be from his informing them, or from their witnessing the conditions of those in their time, and hearing of the conditions of those before them. Or it is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraD*) between the explained part, namely ﴿he warned his people﴾, and the explanatory part, namely His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That you worship none but Allah﴾, for the prohibition of something is a warning of its harm, as if it were said: "And mention the time of Hud's warning to his people with what the messengers before him and after him warned with, namely that you worship none but Allah," indicating that it is a warning that is established, old and new, upon which all the messengers, peace be upon them, agreed without exception. Thus it confirms His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And mention﴾, and confirms His saying, glorified is He: ﴿He warned his people﴾. For this reason it is placed in the middle. It is also intended for mention, unlike when it is made a *hal*, for then it is a subordinate qualifier. This view is preferable to the previous one according to what was established in *al-Kashf*. Some permitted that it be conjoined with *andhara*, meaning: "and inform them of that." But this is as you see. *An* was made *mufassirah* (explanatory) because the meaning of speech preceded without its letters, namely the warning, and the explained element is its implied object. It was also permitted that it be *masdariyyah* (verbal) and that it be *mukhaffafah* (a lightened form) from *al-thaqilah* (the heavy form), in which case before it is an implied preposition connected with *andhir*, meaning: "warn them that you worship none but Allah."

﴿Indeed I fear for you the punishment of a great day﴾. This is an attribute of *yawm* (day), and its greatness is a metaphor for its being terrifying, because that is necessarily connected to it. The day being terrifying is in view of the terror of the punishment in it, so the attribution is figurative. There is no need to make it an attribute of the punishment. The genitive is by proximity (*jarr li-l-jiwar*). The sentence is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*) giving the reason for the prohibition. It is understood: "I fear for you that because of your polytheism."

They said: "Have you come to us to turn us away from our gods?" — an interrogative of reproach. ﴿To turn us away﴾, i.e., to divert us, as al-Dahhak said, from ifk (ifk here in the sense of sarf, turning away). It was also said: it means "to bring us down with a lie", ifk being falsehood (al-kadhib). ﴿From our gods﴾, i.e., from worshipping them. ﴿So bring us what you threaten us with﴾ of hastening the punishment for shirk in this world, ﴿if you are of the truthful﴾ in your promise of its descent upon us.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 46, verse 23:

﴿He said: "The knowledge is only with Allah"﴾, meaning: the knowledge of its time of descent, or the knowledge of all things, of which that is a part, is with Allah alone; I have no knowledge of the time of its descent. The statement is a kinaya (metonymy) for the fact that he has no power over it, nor over hastening it, for if he had power over it and willed it, he would have some knowledge of it in general. Thus, the negation of his knowledge of it, implied by the restrictive construction, is a negation of his having any role in it, so that he would seek its hastening from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and call upon Him for it.

By this explanation it becomes clear that his peace be upon him, his answer corresponds to their saying: (Bring us what you threaten, and He will bring it to you at its appointed time), ﴿and I convey to you what I have been sent with﴾, which is among the obligations of the messengership, of which part is the clarification of the descent of the punishment, since you have not desisted from shirk. Abu 'Amr read (ublighukum) from al-iblagh (conveying).

﴿But I see you as a people who are ignorant﴾, ignorance is your condition, and among its effects is that you propose to him what is not among the functions of the messengers, namely bringing the punishment.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 46, verse 24:

The fa' (fa') in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So when they saw it as a cloud﴾, is fasihah (an elliptical fa', indicating an omitted clause), meaning: then he came to them, so when they saw it. The pronoun of accusative (the object pronoun, "it") is said to refer to (ma) in ﴿what you threaten us with﴾. The thing seen being the thing promised is taken in terms of its outcome and its being a cause of it; otherwise it is not literally the thing seen. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be mubham (undetermined, unspecified), explained by ﴿as a cloud﴾, which is either a tamyiz (specification) or a hal (circumstantial accusative). Then he said: "This aspect is a'rab" — that is, clearer and more manifest — "because of what we pointed to in the first aspect of obscurity, and more eloquent because of the clarity it has after ambiguity; and clarification after concealment is more effective."

Abu Hayyan criticized him, saying that the undetermined term which the tamyiz explains and clarifies occurs only in the chapter of rubba, such as rubbahu rajulan laqitahu, and in the chapter of ni'ma and bi'sa according to the Basran school, such as ni'ma rajulan Zaydun and bi'sa ghulaman 'Amrun. As for the claim that the hal clarifies and explains the undetermined, we know of no one who held it. The grammarians have restricted the pronoun that is explained by what follows it, and they did not mention among them the object of ra'a (to see) when it is a pronoun, nor that the hal explains and clarifies the pronoun. You know the eminence of Jar Allah and his imamate in Arabic.

Al-'arid (the cloud) is the cloud that spreads across the horizon of the sky, and from it is the saying of the poet:

O you who saw a cloud, for which I kept vigil, between the two forelegs and forehead of a lion,

and the saying of al-A'sha:

O you who saw a cloud which I have kept watching, as if the lightning in its edges were torches.

﴿facing their valleys﴾, that is, heading toward their valleys and opposite them. (Awdiyah) is the plural of wad (valley), and the pattern af'ilah for the plural of fa'il is irregular as a noun, such as nad and andiyah (assembly), and permissible for the extended wooden beam at the top of the ceiling, and ajwizah. The idafah (construction) is lafziyyah (verbal, not genuine), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "This is a cloud bringing us rain"﴾; and for this reason both occur as adjectives of an indefinite noun. Al-Zamakhshari described it as majaziyyah (figurative). The basis of the figurative usage is that this idafah serves for expansion and lightening, since it conveys no additional meaning beyond what was before; so just as treating the adverbial of place as the object is figurative, so too treating the object or the subject as the object of idafah in specificity is figurative. It was not intended that they are of the category of idafah due to the slightest connection.

﴿Rather, it is what you hastened for﴾, that is, of the punishment. The speech is on the presumption of a saying before it, that is: Hud said, "Rather, it is..." because the address was between him and them previously. This is supported by the fact that it was read thus. Some of them estimated it as "Say, rather, it is...", for the reading with it as well, and for the need for that because it is an idrab (a turning away from a prior statement), and it cannot be part of the speech of those who said "This is a cloud bringing us rain." Al-Baghawi estimated "Allah said, rather, it is...", and the sublime composition is disjoined by it, as is not hidden. It was read "Rather, what you hastened" (ma is in the accusative as object, in the sense "rather, it [is]"), and a group read "what you were hastened" with a dammah on the ta' and kasrah on the jim. ﴿A wind﴾ is a badal (substitute) for (ma), or for (huwa), or a khabar (predicate) of an omitted mubtada' (subject), that is: it is, or he is, a wind. ﴿In it is a painful punishment﴾ is a sifah (adjective) of (wind), because it is a sentence following an indefinite noun; and likewise His saying, exalted is He,

*Ruh al-Ma'ani* (al-Alusi), commentary on Surah 46, verse 25:

﴿تُدَمِّرُ﴾, meaning it destroys, ﴿كُلَّ شَيْءٍ﴾, everything, from their selves and their wealth, or of what it was commanded to destroy, ﴿بِأمْرِ رَبِّها﴾, by the command of its Lord. It may also be a new sentence (*mustanaf*, a resumptive clause). Zayd ibn 'Ali read *tadmuru* with a fatha on the *ta'*, a sukun on the *dal*, and a damma on the *mim*. It was also read in the same way but with a *ya'* (*yadmuru*), with *kullun* in the nominative as the subject of *yudammiru*, which comes from *dammara*, *damaran*, meaning he perished. In that case the clause is also a qualifier (*sifa*), and the returning pronoun is omitted, meaning *bi-ha* (by it), or the pronoun in *rabbiha* refers back. It may also be a new sentence, as in the reading of the majority. He intended to explain that every contingent thing has a fixed, appointed time, bound to the command of its Creator, which neither advances nor delays. The pronoun in *rabbiha* refers to "everything," for it carries the sense of "things." The mention of the *amr* (command), the *Rabb* (Lord), and the attribution to the wind shows, in ways that are not hidden, the greatness of His majesty (*'azza wa jall*).

The *fa'* in His words, exalted is He, ﴿فَأصْبَحُوا لا يُرى إلا مَساكِنُهُمْ﴾, meaning *so they became such that nothing was seen but their dwellings*, is *fa' fasiha* (the eloquent *fa'*, which indicates an omitted clause). That is: the wind came upon them, and it destroyed them, so that nothing was seen but their dwellings. Some of them made it the *fa' al-ta'qib* (the *fa'* of immediate sequence), on the basis of an implied *qawl* (saying) attributed to Him, exalted is He, and claimed that there is no actual saying here, but rather it is an expression for the speed of their annihilation and the occurrence of their destruction without delay. This, as you see, is [unconvincing].

The majority read *la tara* (you do not see) with the *ta'* of address, and *illa masakinahum* (except their dwellings) with the accusative. The address is to everyone who is capable of seeing, as an alert that their condition is such that if everyone were to come to their land, he would see nothing but their dwellings. Or it is addressed to the master of those addressed, ﷺ.

Abu Raja', Malik ibn Dinar (with a variant from both of them), al-Jahdari, al-A'mash, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and al-Sulami read *la tura* with a *ta'* above the line, with a damma, and *illa masakinuhum* with the nominative. Most grammarians hold that feminine agreement is not permitted when separated by *illa* (except), except in poetry, as in the words of Dhu al-Rummah:

*Ka-annahu jamalun hamma wa-ma baqiyat*
*illa al-nahiza wa al-alwahu wa al-'asabu*

It is as if it were a camel that had perished, and nothing remained but its breastbone, its ribs, and its sinews.

And the words of another, which Ibn Jinni attributed also to Dhu al-Rummah:

*Bara al-nahza wa al-ajrala ma fi ghuruḍiha*
*wa-ma baqiyat illa al-ḍulu'u al-jarashi'u*

It wore away the lean flesh and the hind-legs, and what was in its ... [its] ribs, and nothing remained but the protruding ribs.

Some of them permit it without restriction. The full discussion of this belongs in its proper place. Isa al-Hamdani read *la yura* with a damma on the *ya'* below the line (*yu'ra*, passive), *illa maskanuhum* in the singular and nominative, and this was narrated from al-A'mash and Nasr ibn 'Asim. It was also read *la tara* with an open *ta'* above the line, *illa maskanahum* in the singular and accusative. This is the singular that is intended as a plural, or a verbal noun (*masdar*) whose genitive has been omitted, meaning *the traces of their dwelling*.

﴿كَذَلِكَ﴾, that is, like that dreadful recompense, ﴿نَجْزِي القَوْمَ المُجْرِمِينَ﴾, We recompense the guilty people.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *Kitab al-Sahab*, and Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azamah*, narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he said regarding His words, exalted is He, ﴿فَلَمّا رَأوْهُ﴾ (When they saw it), the verse: the first thing by which they knew that it was a punishment was that they saw what used to be carried off from their camp and their livestock flying between the sky and the earth like feathers. So they entered their houses and closed their doors. Then the wind came, opened their doors, and poured the sand upon them, so they were under the sand for seven nights and eight days, in continuous succession, with moaning among them. Then Allah commanded the wind, and it cleared the sand from them and threw them into the sea. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿فَأصْبَحُوا لا يُرى إلا مَساكِنُهُمْ﴾.

It is narrated that the first of them to see the punishment was a woman, who saw a wind in which were sparks like shooting flames. It is also narrated that when Hud, peace be upon him, sensed the wind, he drew a line around himself and the believers, beside a spring that was flowing. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he, peace be upon him, withdrew with those who were with him into an enclosure, so that the wind did not reach them except as much as softens the skins and pleases the souls. It would pass over the people of 'Ad with their caravans between the sky and the earth, and strike them with stones. It was, as Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Jarir narrated from 'Amr ibn Maymun, bringing back a man who was absent. What has passed concerning them in Surah al-A'raf is enough; return to it if you wish. Because of what the wind had brought upon them, he (ﷺ) used to supplicate whenever the wind blew strongly.

Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, and 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "When the wind blew strongly, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would say: 'O Allah, I ask You for its good, the good within it, and the good for which it was sent, and I seek refuge in You from its evil, the evil within it, and the evil for which it was sent.' When the sky became overcast, his complexion would change (ﷺ), and he would go out and come in, advance and withdraw. When it rained, his anxiety would be relieved. I asked him about this, and he (ﷺ) said: 'I do not know, perhaps it is as the people of 'Ad said: *This is a cloud bringing us rain*.'"

﴿Indeed, We had established them﴾, that is, We had established ʿĀd and empowered them. The *mā* in His words ﴿in that wherein We had established you﴾ is either a relative pronoun, or a relative pronoun, and *in* (*in*) is a negation. That is: in that which, or in something, We had established you in, of abundance, stature, long lives, and all the other means of control, as in His words ﴿How many generations before them did We destroy, whom We had established on earth as We have not established you?﴾. The negation was not expressed with the word *mā* out of dislike of repeating the word, even though the meaning differs. For this reason, those who held that the original form of *mahmā* is *mā mā*, with the conditional *mā* repeated for emphasis, changed the first *alif* into a *hāʾ* to avoid the repetition. They criticized al-Mutanabbi for his words:

"By your life, what has been separated from you by a striker is no more deadly than what has been separated from you by a critic."

That is: "what is it that has been separated from you," etc. He means that his tongue does not fall short of his spear: this (tongue) is for the critic, and that (spear) is for the striker. He could have said: "Indeed what has been separated," and inserting the *bāʾ* is for negation, not for governing, since the governing function of *in* has come from al-Mubarrad. It has also been said that *in* is a conditional with its response omitted,
[Page 28]
and the estimate is: "If We had established you in it, you would have rebelled." It has also been said that it is a connective particle after the relative *mā*, made similar to the negative *mā* and the temporal *mā*. So in the verse it is like it in his words:

"A man hopes for what he will not see, and calamities stand between him and its nearest approach."

That is: We had established them in the like of that wherein We had established you. That it is negative is the most apparent view, because the Mighty Qur'an indicates it in many places, and it is more eloquent in rebuke and more effective in urging reflection.

﴿And We made for them hearing, sight and hearts﴾, so that they would use them for what they were created for, and know through each of them what its knowledge was attached to, of the varieties of blessings, and infer through them the affairs of their Bestower, the Mighty, the Majestic, and persist in thanking Him, exalted is His majesty.

﴿But their hearing availed them not﴾, in that they did not use it to listen to revelation and the admonitions of the Messengers. ﴿Nor their sight﴾, in that they did not behold through it the created signs inscribed in the pages of the world. ﴿Nor their hearts﴾, in that they did not use them to know God, exalted is He. ﴿Of anything﴾, that is, any amount of benefit. (*Min*) is redundant for emphasis, and the tanwīn is for diminution.

It is also permitted that it be partitive, meaning: it did not avail some of the availing, namely a little. The *mā* in ﴿So availed not﴾ is negative, and it is permitted that it be interrogative. Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying that it would entail the addition of (*min*) in an affirmative context, which is not permitted according to the correct view. It was answered that they said it may be added in a non-affirmative context, and they explained that as negation, prohibition and interrogation. The singular "hearing" in this sublime wording and the plural of the others is because what is perceived by it is one kind, namely sounds, while the objects perceived by the others are multiple; or because it is originally a verbal noun. Also, what they heard from the Messengers was one.

﴿Since they used to deny the signs of God﴾: a temporal clause connected to the explicit or implicit negation in His words ﴿availed not﴾. It is a temporal clause intended to express causation, either metonymically or figuratively, since the meaning of the temporal clause and of causation is equivalent in your saying: "I struck him for his offence" and "I struck him when he offended," because you struck him at that time due to the presence of the offence in it. This is one of the usages that prevailed for *idh* and *ḥaythu* among all the temporal particles, until it almost came to be counted among their original lexical meanings.

﴿And there befell them what they used to mock﴾: of the punishment which they were hastening by way of mockery, and they would say: ﴿Bring us what you promise us, if you are of the truthful﴾.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 46, verse 27:

﴿And We did destroy what is around you﴾ O people of Makkah, ﴿of the towns﴾ like the rocky tract of Thamud and the towns of the people of Salih. The speech is either by way of an elided noun (i.e., "the people of the towns"), or the "towns" are used figuratively for their inhabitants. [Compare] His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We varied the signs﴾, meaning We repeated them, ﴿so that they might return﴾. The matter of "ma" is easy, and the "hope" (taraji) is turned toward others than Him, exalted is He; or "la'alla" is for causation, meaning: so that they might return from what they are in of disbelief and sins to faith and obedience.
