﴿فَلَوْلا نَصَرَهُمُ﴾ Why then did they not help them? That is, why did they not prevent them from the destruction into which they had fallen? ﴿الَّذِينَ اتَّخَذُوا﴾ "Those who had taken," that is, their gods, whom they had taken.

﴿مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ قُرْبانًا آلِهَةً﴾ The pronoun we supposed to refer back is the first object (*maf'ūl awwal*) of *ittakhadhū* ("they took"). *Āliha* ("gods") is the second object (*maf'ūl thānī*). *Qurbānan*, meaning "a means of drawing near," is a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*). The sense is: they took them as gods besides God, in a state in which they were a means of drawing near to God, Mighty and Majestic, as they used to say: ﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us near to God in closeness﴾ and ﴿These are our intercessors with God﴾. There is also a mocking tone toward them in the statement.

Al-Ḥawfī permitted *qurbānan* to be an object of purpose (*maf'ūl li-ajlihi*). He, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Makkī and Abū al-Baqāʾ also permitted it to be the second object of *ittakhadhū*, and made *āliha* a substitute (*badal*) for it. Al-Zamakhsharī said in *al-Kashshāf*: "This is not valid, because the meaning is corrupt." It is also reported from him in his *Bayān* that it is not valid to say: "They took them as a means of drawing near, apart from God," because God, Exalted, is not drawn near to by them. What he meant, as in *al-Kashf*, is this: if it is made a second object, the meaning becomes: "Why did those who took them as a means of drawing near in place of God, or who went beyond taking God as a means of drawing near to them, not help them?" And this is a corrupt meaning.

It was objected to this by making *dūna* mean "in front of" (*qudām*), as has been said of His words: ﴿Call your witnesses apart from God﴾, and by saying that *qurbānan* has been said to be an object of purpose, which is not restricted to what is drawn near to, and it may be applied to what one draws near to; in that case the sentence is coherent.

It is answered regarding the first point that it is not a damaging objection: despite the rarity of using *dūna* to mean "in front of," the verb of taking cannot take it as its adverbial location (*ẓarf*), because one does not take something "in front of God." Rather, drawing near is done in front of Him and for His sake. Their taking of them as a means of drawing near is not drawing near to God, because its meaning is exalting them through worship so that they might intercede before God, Mighty and Majestic, and bring them close to Him, Glorified. Thus the time of taking is not at all the time of drawing near. In that case, if it were a stable circumstance (*ḥāl mustaqirr*), what was entailed in the first case would follow.

It is not permissible for *qurbānan* to govern anything, because it is an inert noun (*ism jāmid*) meaning "that by which one draws near," so it is not fit to be an operative word, like *al-qārūrah* ("the flask"), even though it carries the meaning of settling. There is room for consideration in this.

It is answered regarding the second point that al-Zamakhsharī, after explaining *qurbān* as "that by which one draws near," mentioned this prohibition, although His words after ﴿Rather, they have strayed from them﴾ etc. loudly proclaim the corruption of that.

Some have said, regarding the impossibility of *qurbānan* being a second object with *āliha* as its substitute, that a substitute, though it is the intended element, must in a non-substitute of error (*badal al-ghalaṭ*) have a correct meaning without it. There is no validity to their saying "They took them apart from God as a means of drawing near," meaning "that by which one draws near," because God, Exalted, is not drawn near to by it; rather one draws near to Him. So it is not valid to say that they took them as a means of drawing near, going beyond God in that. Some inclined to the view that it is valid to say: "God is drawn near to by it," meaning by His pleasure and by seeking a means through Him, Exalted.

Al-Ṭībī said: al-Zamakhsharī did not intend by the corruption of the meaning anything but the opposite of the intended meaning, since their purpose in taking the idols as gods, according to their claim, was nothing but that they should draw near to God, Exalted, as the verses declare. So reflect.

It is read *qurubānan* with a damma on the *rāʾ*. ﴿Rather, they strayed from them﴾, that is, they were absent from them. There is also mockery of them in this, as if their not helping them was due to their absence, or they were lost to them, meaning their loss became entirely evident to them, and the help they had been hoping for was ruled out, like the help of an absent one for the one who is to be helped.

﴿And that﴾, that is, the straying of their gods from them, ﴿was their falsehood﴾, that is, the effect of their falsehood, meaning their turning away from the truth, and their taking them as gods, and the outcome of their polytheism. ﴿And what they used to fabricate﴾, that is, the effect of their fabrication and their lying against God, Exalted; or the effect of what they used to fabricate against God, Mighty and Majestic. It is also said that *dhālika* refers to the taking of the idols as gods, meaning: that taking, whose effect was the straying of their gods from them, was their lying and fabrication. Or: and what they used to fabricate, though this is not that, even if it does not require supposing an elided genitive (*muḍāf*).

Ibn ʿAbbās, in one transmission, read *afkuhum* with a fatḥa on the *hamza*. *Al-ifk* and *al-afk* are both verbal nouns, like *al-ḥadhar* and *al-ḥadhar*. Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Ṣabbāḥ ibn al-ʿAlāʾ al-Anṣārī, Abū ʿIyāḍ, ʿIkrimah, Ḥanṭalah ibn al-Nuʿmān ibn Murrah, and Mujāhid read *afaka-hum* with three fatḥas, taking *afaka* as a past verb. In that case the reference of "that" is to the taking: that taking turned them away from the truth.

﴿And what they were﴾: it is said to be coordinated with "that," or with the hidden pronoun, and this is good because of the separation. Or it is a subject (*mubtadaʾ*) whose predicate is elided, meaning "likewise." In that case the sentence is coordinated with the sentence before it.

Abū ʿIyāḍ and ʿIkrimah also read it that way, except that they doubled the *fāʾ* for intensification. Ibn al-Zubayr also, and Ibn ʿAbbās as reported by Ibn Khalawayh, read *āfakuhum* with a long vowel. This may be a *fāʿala* form, with the *hamza* original; or an *afʿala* form, with the *hamza* for causation, meaning "He made them turn away." It is also permitted that it be for finding (*lil-wijdān*), like *aḥmadtuhu* ("I found him praiseworthy"), or that it be *afʿala* with the meaning of *faʿala*. It is reported in *al-Baḥr* that it was read *afakuhum* with a fatḥa on the *hamza* and *fāʾ* and a ḍamma on the *kāf*, which is a dialect form for *al-ifk*. Ibn ʿAbbās, as transmitted by Quṭrub and Abū al-Faḍl al-Rāzī, read *āfakahum*, an active participle from *afaka*, meaning: that taking is what turns them away from the truth.

It is read *wa-dhālika ifkun mimmā kānū yaftarūn* ("That is a falsehood of what they used to fabricate"). The meaning is: that is part of what they fabricate of falsehood, that is, part of their fabricated lies. Thus *al-ifk* carries the meaning of "lying." So do not be heedless.

And [mention] when We turned toward you a company of jinn (nafar) listening to the Qur'an. That is, We inclined them toward you and directed them to you. The nafar (a small group), according to the well-known view, is from three to ten men, because it derives from nafir (mobilization), and men are those who, when a matter confronts them, mobilize to meet it. The truth is that this applies to the majority of cases, for in eloquent usage it is also applied to groups above ten, and a number of lexicographers have mentioned this. In summary, rahṭ and nafar are used up to forty. In the speech of al-Sha'bi: "He related to me a dozen nafar." It will come, God willing, that this verse is to be interpreted here as more than ten, and that it is not restricted to men. Deriving it from nafir does not indicate restriction to men, nor even to people, since it is applied here to the jinn.

The prepositional phrase (al-jar wa-al-majrur) is a qualifier of "nafar." His statement, "listening to the Qur'an," is a hal muqaddarah (an anticipated circumstantial clause) qualifying it, because it has been specified by the qualifier, or it is another qualifier of it. The plural pronoun is used because nafar is an ism jam' (collective noun), so in meaning it is plural. For this reason, "ṣarrafnā" was read with shadda (doubling), for intensification. "Idh" (when) governs an implied verb; it is not coordinated with "akhā ʿĀd" (the brother of ʿĀd). The meaning is: "Mention to your people the time when We turned toward you a company of jinn, intending that they listen to the Qur'an, so that they might become aware of their ignorance, their error, and the ugliness of their disbelief in the Qur'an and their turning away from it, since they disbelieved in it and were ignorant that it was from God Most High. Yet they are the people of the tongue in which it was revealed, and of the same kind as the Messenger who brought it. Those [jinn] listened to it, knew that it was from Him, Exalted, and believed in it, though they are not of its tongue's people nor of the same kind as its Messenger. Therefore, in the mention of this story there is a rebuke to the disbelievers of Quraysh and the Arabs." Its placement immediately after the story of Hud and his people and the destruction of those destroyed among the people of the settlements is because those people were of great strength and power, as is related of them in more than one verse, and the jinn are also described with this, as He, Exalted, said: "An ʿIfrit of the jinn said, 'I will bring it to you before you rise from your place, and indeed I am strong and trustworthy for it.'" Their being described thus is well known among the Arabs. So it is appropriate to what precedes it, along with what has been said: that the story of ʿĀd includes the mention of the wind, and this one includes the mention of the jinn, and both are from the unseen world that is not witnessed. The discussion of their reality will come.

﴿Then when they attended it﴾, that is, the Qur'an at the time of its recitation. This is the apparent meaning, though there is some figurative usage in it. It has been said that the Messenger (ﷺ) was reciting it to them, and so there is an iltifat (shift in grammatical person) in it.

"They said" — that is, some of them said to others: "Be silent [anṣitū] so that we may hear it." In this there is a lesson in good manners with knowledge, and in how it is to be learned. "When it was concluded" — that is, when he had completed and finished its recitation. Abu Mijlaz and Habib ibn Abdullah read (qaḍā) with the verb in the active voice, its subject being the pronoun of the Messenger, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and by this they strengthen the return of the pronoun in "attended it" (ḥaḍarūhu) to him, upon him be blessings and peace.

"They turned back to their people as warners" — intending to warn them upon their arrival to them. It is said that they dispersed throughout the lands and warned whomever of the jinn they met. These, as is mentioned in several reports, were jinn of Nasibin, which is among the lands of Bakr, close to Syria. It is also said they were from Nineveh, which is likewise among the lands of Bakr, but close to Mosul. It is mentioned that they were of the Shaysaban, who are the most numerous of the jinn, and the bulk of Iblis's soldiers are from them. The gathering took place in the valley of Nakhla, about a night's journey from blessed Mecca. Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim), al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and a group [of compilers] have transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, set out with a company of his Companions toward the market of Ukaz, and the devils had been prevented from the news of the heavens, and shooting stars were sent upon them. The devils returned to their people and said, 'What is wrong with you?' They said, 'We have been prevented from the news of the heavens, and shooting stars have been sent upon us.' They said, 'Nothing has come between you and the news of the heavens except that something has happened. Strike the eastern and western parts of the earth and see what this is that has come between you and the news of the heavens.' So those who had headed toward Tihama turned back to the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, while he and his Companions were at Nakhla, intending for the market of Ukaz; he, upon him be blessings and peace, was leading his Companions in the dawn prayer. When they heard the Qur'an, they listened to it, and then they said, 'By Allah, this is what has come between you and the news of the heavens.' Then, when they returned to their people, [it was then]."

In the narration of Ibn al-Mundhir from Abd al-Malik: when they attended it, they said, "Be silent." When he, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, had concluded and finished the dawn prayer, they turned back to their people as believing warners, and he was not aware of them until there was revealed: "Say: It has been revealed to me that a company of the jinn listened..."

In the Two Sahihs, from Masruq, from Ibn Mas'ud: a tree informed the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, of them. They were, according to what is reported from Ibn Abbas, seven; Zirr also said so and mentioned Zawba'a among them. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid that they were seven: three from the people of Harran and four from Nasibin, and their names were Hasa, Masa, Shasir, Masir, al-Urduwaniyyan, Sarq and al-Ahqam (with a final mim); in another report from Ka'b it is al-Ahqab (with a ba'). The author of al-Rawd mentioned, in place of Hasa and Masa, Munshi' and Nashi'. Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Abbas that he said concerning these company: they were nineteen, from the people of Nasibin, and the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, made them messengers to their people. The preceding report indicates that the jinn attended while he, upon him be blessings, was with a company of his Companions. Abd ibn Humayd, Ahmad, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud transmitted from Alqama, who said: "I said to Ibn Mas'ud: Did any one of you accompany the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, on the night of the jinn? He said: No one of us accompanied him, but we were with the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, one night, and we lost him, so we searched for him in the valleys and the mountain passes, and we said: He has been carried off or assassinated. We spent the worst night any people ever spent, and when we awoke, behold, he came from the direction of Hira. We informed him, and he said: 'The caller of the jinn came to me, so I went to them and recited the Qur'an to them.' Then he set off with us and showed us their traces and the traces of their fires." This indicates that he, upon him be blessings and peace, had no one of his Companions with him, and none of them was aware of him.

Ahmad transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "I stood with the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, on the night of the jinn, and I took a water-skin, and I do not think it contained anything but water. When we were at the top of Mecca, I saw black shapes gathered together. He said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, drew a line for me and said: 'Stand here until I come to you.' The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, went to them, and I saw them rushing toward him. He conversed with them through the long night until he came to me at dawn and said: 'Do you have any water for ablution?' I said: 'Yes,' and I opened the water-skin, and behold, it was nabidh. I said: 'I did not think it was anything but water.' The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, said: 'A good date and pure water.' He performed ablution with it, then stood to pray. Two of them came to him, and he placed them behind him, and then he led us in prayer. I said: 'Who are these, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'Jinn of Nasibin.'"

This indicates something contrary to what preceded, and it is reconciled by the multiplicity of the occasions of the jinn's coming. Al-Tabarani in al-Awsat and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from the Rabbi (Ibn Abbas) that he said: "The jinn were turned toward the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, twice." Al-Khafaji mentioned that the hadiths indicate that the delegations of the jinn were six times, and by this the differences in the reports about their number and other matters are reconciled. Abu Nu'aym and al-Waqidi transmitted from Ka'b al-Ahbar, who said: "The nine men of the jinn of Nasibin departed from the valley of Nakhla, namely so-and-so, so-and-so, so-and-so, the two Urduwaniyyan and al-Ahqab, and they came to their people as warners. Afterward they went out as a delegation to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and they were three hundred. They reached al-Hajun, and al-Ahqab came and greeted the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and said: 'Our people have come to al-Hajun to meet you.' The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, made an appointment with him for an hour of the night at al-Hajun."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ikrima that he said concerning the verse: "They were twelve thousand from the island of Mosul." The Kashshaf also mentions this number, and that the surah which the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, recited to them was "Read in the name of your Lord." In al-Bahr it is reported from Ibn Umar and Jabir ibn Abdullah, may Allah be pleased with them, that he, upon him be blessings and peace, recited to them Surah al-Rahman, and whenever he said, "So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?" they said: "None of the blessings of our Lord do we deny; to You belongs all praise." Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il and al-Waqidi transmitted from Abu Ja'far, who said: "The jinn came to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, in Rabi' al-Awwal of the eleventh year of prophethood." In a similar sense it has been said: the incident was three years before the Hijra, based on what is authentically reported from Ibn Abbas that the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, remained in Mecca receiving revelation for thirteen years. There is disagreement on this matter, and what is well known is what has been mentioned.

It has been said: the listening of the jinn occurred at the beginning of the revelation. "They said" — that is, upon their return to their people — "O our people, we have heard a Book" of great standing "that has been sent down after Musa," they mentioned it without mentioning Isa, peace be upon them both, because that is agreed upon among the People of the Two Scriptures, and because the Book sent down to Musa is the greatest of the books before the Qur'an, and Isa, peace be upon him, was commanded to act upon most of it or all of it. 'Ata' said: because they were upon Judaism, and it requires a sound transmission. It is reported from Ibn Abbas that the jinn had not heard of the affair of Isa, peace be upon him, which is why they said that. But this is remote, for the fame of the affair of Isa, peace be upon him, and the spread of the matter of his religion is too evident to be hidden, especially from the jinn. For this reason Abu Hayyan said: this is not sound from Ibn Abbas. "Confirming what is before it" — of the Torah, or of all the previous divine books — "it guides to the truth" — of the correct beliefs — "and to a straight path" — of the practical rulings, or what encompasses them and other matters of belief, on the basis that this is the mention of the general after the specific.

O our people, respond to the caller of Allah ﴿يا قَوْمَنا أجِيبُوا داعِيَ اللَّهِ﴾. They meant by this what they had heard of the Book, and they described it as a call to Allah, the Exalted, after describing it as guidance to the truth and the straight path, because the two entail each other. Joining the two together is an extremely strong encouragement to them to respond. It is also permissible that by "the caller of Allah" they meant the Messenger (ﷺ). ﴿وآمِنُوا بِهِ﴾ "and believe in him," i.e., in the caller of Allah, the Exalted, or in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. ﴿يَغْفِرْ لَكم مِن ذُنُوبِكُمْ﴾ "He will forgive you of your sins," i.e., some of your sins. It was said: these are the ones that concern only the right of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for the rights of people are not forgiven by faith alone. Ibn al-Munir objected to this, saying that if a ḥarbī (a non-Muslim at war with the Muslims) plunders wealth and sheds blood and then his Islam is good, his Islam clearly erases the sin of what preceded it. He then said: "It is said that the promise of forgiveness, on condition of faith, has not come in the Book of Allah for the disbelievers except in a partial form. If there is no secret in its being consistently so, then the matter is simply that the station of the disbelievers is one of restriction (qabḍ), not expansion (basṭ), and therefore their hope for the forgiveness of all their sins has not been expanded, whereas it has come regarding the believers many times." Ṣāḥib al-Inṣāf replied to this by saying that the station of encouraging the disbeliever to Islam is one of expansion, not restriction, and Allah the Exalted commanded that Pharaoh be spoken to ﴿قَوْلا لَيِّنًا﴾ "with gentle speech." Allah the Exalted also said: ﴿إنْ يَنْتَهُوا يُغْفَرْ لَهم ما قَدْ سَلَفَ﴾ "If they desist, what has already passed will be forgiven them," and this is not partial, and (ما) is for generality, especially since it occurs in a conditional clause.

Some of the eminent verifiers said: although the ḥarbī, when he becomes Muslim, has no liability left upon him at all, the dhimmī (a non-Muslim living under Muslim protection) who becomes Muslim still retains the rights of human beings. The people in question, as reported from ʿAṭāʾ, were Jews, so their obligations to one another remain upon them if they all become Muslim without war. Since the address was with them, something indicating partiality was brought. It was also said: it was brought because the jinn did not yet know that Islam erases the sin of what came before it absolutely, though this is open to question. It may be said: they meant by "some" the past sins. Had they not said that, the listeners might have supposed that if they responded to the caller of Allah, the Exalted, and believed in him, all their past and future sins would be forgiven them. It was also said: min (in مِن) is extra, meaning: He will forgive you your sins. ﴿ويُجِرْكم مِن عَذابٍ ألِيمٍ﴾ "and protect you from a painful punishment," which is prepared for the disbelievers. This and similar statements indicate that the jinn are obligated (mukallafūn), but nothing has been stated here about their reward if they obey. The general statements of the verses indicate reward. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās: "They have reward and they have punishment; they will meet in Paradise and crowd at its gates." Perhaps the limitation here to what has been mentioned is because it contains a reminder of sins, and the context is one of warning, so nothing of reward was mentioned in it. It was also said: there is no reward for those among them who obey except salvation from the Fire, and it will be said to them: "Be dust," and they will become dust. This is the view of Layth ibn Abī Sulaym and a group, and it is attributed to Imam Abū Ḥanīfa, may Allah be pleased with him. al-Nasafī said in al-Taysīr: Abū Ḥanīfa hesitated concerning the reward of the jinn in Paradise and their bliss, because there is no entitlement for a servant upon Allah, the Exalted, and he did not state, by way of promise concerning them, anything except forgiveness and protection from punishment. As for the bliss of Paradise, it depends on evidence.

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said: the believing jinn are around Paradise in its outskirts (rabaḍ), and they are not within it. It was also said: they enter Paradise and are inspired to glorify and remember Allah, and so they obtain from the pleasure of that what the children of Adam obtain from their delights. al-Nawawī said in his commentary on Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim: "The correct view is that they enter it and enjoy its bounties by eating, drinking and other things." This is the view of al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Mālik ibn Anas, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ibn Abī Layla and others.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 46, verse 32:

﴿And whoever does not respond to the caller of Allah, then he cannot escape (Allah) on earth.﴾ This is an obligation to respond, expressed in the mode of warning (tarhib), following its obligation expressed in the mode of encouragement (targhib); and it confirms that they are warners. The mention of "the caller of Allah" in full, rather than suffice with one of the two pronouns, is by saying "yajib-hu" or "yujib dā'iyahu," for the sake of emphasis in the obligation, by adding affirmation, cultivating awe, and instilling dread.

The restriction of the inability (to escape) to being "on earth" serves to widen the scope; that is, he cannot escape from Allah the Exalted by fleeing, even if he flees every way out of its regions or enters its depths.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And he will have no protectors besides Him﴾ is an explanation of the impossibility of his being saved through another, following the explanation of the impossibility of his being saved by himself. The plural "protectors" (awliya') is in view of the meaning of "min" (from/any), so it falls under the category of matching plural with plural, since the individuals are distributed among the individuals. This is supported by what is reported from Ibn 'Amir that he recited "wa-laysa lahum" with the plural pronoun, for "min" in the sense of its meaning. Likewise the plural in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Those﴾ is in view of that same consideration, i.e., those described by not responding to the caller of Allah ﴿are in clear error﴾, meaning their being in error is evident, such that it is not hidden from anyone, since they turned away from responding to one of such a station.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 46, verse 33:**

﴿Do they not see﴾. The hamza (the interrogative particle) expresses denial (inkar), and the waw, according to one of the two opinions, is a conjunction (ʿatf) coordinating with an implied clause that the interrogative (istifham) has entered, which the context calls for. The seeing (al-ru'yah) is of the heart, meaning: "Have they not reflected and not known" ﴿that Allah, who created the heavens and the earth, and was not wearied by their creation﴾. That is, He was not fatigued by it at all. It comes from ʿayiya (عَيِيَ), on the pattern of fa'ila with a kasra on the ʿayn, and idgham (assimilation of the doubled letters) is permissible in it with the meaning of ta'iba (تَعِبَ), like a'ya (أعْيا). Al-Kisa'i said: a'yaytu (أعْيَيْتُ) is from tiredness, while ʿayitu (عَيِيتُ) is from the cessation of resources, incapacity, and bewilderment in a matter. They cited the verse:

"They were baffled by their affair, as the dove was baffled by her egg."

Meaning: He was not incapable of creating them, nor was He bewildered about it. Some scholars chose not to distinguish between the two forms. Al-Hasan recited (وَلَمْ يَعِ) with a kasra on the ʿayn and a sukun on the yaʾ. Its explanation is that in the past tense the ʿayn of the root was given a fatha, as they said in baqiya (بَقِيَ) → baqa (بَقى) with a fatha on the qaf and an alif after it, which is the dialect of Tayy. When the past tense was formed on the pattern fa'ila with a fatha on the ʿayn, its present tense was formed on yaf'alu with a kasra on the ʿayn, so it came as yaʿiy. When the jussive particle (al-jazm) entered, it deleted the yaʾ, leaving yaʿi, with the vowel of the yaʾ transferred to the ʿayn, so the yaʾ became sakin.

﴿Able﴾ (bi-qadir) is in the position of the nominative, because it is the predicate of inna (أنَّ). The bāʾ is superfluous (za'idah) in it, and what made its addition acceptable is that what precedes it is in a negative context. Al-Zajjaj permitted, by analogy with this, the expression: "I did not think that anyone was standing (bi-qa'im)." Abu Hayyan said: the correct view is to restrict this to what is attested in usage. So it is as if it were said here: "Is Allah not able ﴿to give life to the dead﴾?" For this reason it is answered with His saying: ﴿Yes, indeed He is over all things Competent﴾, affirming the power in a general way, which serves as proof of the intended meaning. For this reason it has been said: this points to a major premise (kubra) and a minor premise (sughra) that are easy to obtain. It is as if it were said: "The giving of life to the dead is a thing, and every thing is within His power; so it follows that the giving of life to the dead is within His power," and this entails that He, exalted is He, is ﴿able to give life to the dead﴾.

Al-Jahdari, Zayd ibn ʿAli, ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd, ʿIsa, al-Aʿraj in one of the reports from him, and Yaʿqub recited (yaqdir) (يَقْدِرُ) instead of (bi-qadir), in the present tense indicating continuity. This reading, it is said, also agrees with the Uthmanic script (al-rasm al-ʿUthmani).

[Page 34]

﴿And on the Day when those who disbelieve are exposed to the Fire﴾: this is an adverbial phrase of time (*zarf*), whose governing element is an implied verb of saying (*qawl mudmar*), and its content is His saying, ﴿Is this not the truth?﴾. That is, it is said: "On the Day when they are exposed…" and so on. The apparent view is that the clause is parenthetical (*mu'taridah*). It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*), with the implied sense "and it has been said," but this is open to question. The discussion of "exposure" (*'ard*) has already been covered at length. The reference here is to what they will witness at the time of exposure, in its general sense, without any word coming to mind that indicates it, let alone a masculine or feminine form for it, since this is most fitting to its awfulness and grandeur. It has also been said that the reference is to the punishment, by the indication of its being explicitly mentioned, but this is a distant view. In it there is mockery of them and rebuke for their ridicule of God's promise and threat, and their saying: ﴿We will not be punished﴾.

﴿They will say: "Yes, by our Lord"﴾: this is an affirmation of its truth, and they reinforced it with an oath, as though they hoped to be saved by acknowledging its truth, as they did in the world. But how could they hope for that? It is related from al-Hasan that they will indeed be punished in the Fire while being content with that for themselves, acknowledging that it is justice.

﴿He will say: "Taste the punishment because you used to disbelieve"﴾: this is because of your persistence in disbelief in the world. The meaning of the command is humiliation of them, so it is mockery and rebuke; otherwise it would be the obtaining of what is already obtained (*tahsil al-hasil*). It has also been said that it is a command of creation (*amr takwini*), and the intended meaning is the imposition of a punishment other than that in which they already are. But this is not the correct view.

**[p. 34]**

The *fa'* in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So be patient, as the resolute among the Messengers were patient﴾, is connected to an implied conditional clause (*shart muqaddar*), meaning: "Since the outcome of the disbelievers' affair is what has been mentioned, then be patient with what befalls you from them." Or it means: "Since the matter is as you have come to know of His overwhelming power, exalted is He, [then] be patient." Many have permitted that it is coordinating (*'atifa*) this sentence to what preceded, and the causal sense in it is evident. Al-Bahr (*al-Bahr al-Muhit* of Abu Hayyan) restricted it to coordinating this sentence to the report about the disbelievers in the Hereafter, and said: "The meaning between them is connected, as if it were said: 'This is their state, so do not hasten, and be patient, and fear none but God, mighty and majestic.'"

*Al-'azm* is applied to earnestness and striving in a matter, and to patience upon it. The *min* (from) is *bayaniyya* (explicative, specifying the kind), as in His saying, ﴿So avoid the abomination, which is of the idols﴾. The prepositional phrase (*al-jar wa-l-majrur*) is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) for "the Messengers," so that "those of resolve" (*ulu al-'azm*) is a description of all of them. This is the view of Ibn Zayd, al-Jubba'i, and a group, meaning: ﴿So be patient, as the Messengers were patient﴾, those earnest and striving in conveying the revelation, whom nothing diverts from it and nothing turns aside from it, and those who are patient with the command of God, exalted is He, in what He has entrusted to them, or what He has decreed and ordained for them, mighty and majestic, through an intermediary or without one.

From Ata' al-Khurasani, al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl, al-Kalbi, Muqatil, Qatada, Abu al-'Aliya, and Ibn Jurayj, and to this most exegetes have gone: the *min* is *tab'id* (partitive), so the "those of resolve" are some of the Messengers, peace be upon them. Their number and identification have been disputed, according to several opinions. Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: they are eighteen, and they are those mentioned in Surat al-An'am, because He, glorified is He, said after mentioning them: ﴿So follow their guidance﴾. It was said: nine. Noah, peace be upon him, was patient for a long time with the harm of his people. Abraham, peace be upon him, was patient with being cast into the fire. The Sacrificed one, peace be upon him, was patient with what was intended for him of slaughter.

**[p. 35]**

Jacob, peace be upon him, was patient at the loss of his son. Joseph, peace be upon him, was patient with the well and the prison. Job, peace be upon him, was patient with affliction. Moses, peace be upon him, when his people said to him, ﴿Indeed, we are overtaken﴾, he said, ﴿Indeed, my Lord is with me; He will guide me﴾. David, peace be upon him, wept over his sin for forty years. Jesus, peace be upon him, did not lay one brick upon another, and said: "Indeed, it, meaning the world, is a passage, so cross it and do not settle in it." It was said: seven: Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, David, Solomon, and Jesus, peace be upon them. It was said: six, and they are those who were commanded to fight: Noah, Hud, Salih, Moses, David, and Solomon. Ibn Mardawayh transmitted it from Ibn 'Abbas. From Muqatil, they are six, but he did not mention the hadith of the command to fight, and he said: they are Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, and Job. Ibn 'Asakir transmitted from Qatada that they are Noah, Hud, Abraham, Shu'ayb, and Moses, peace be upon them, and its apparent meaning is the view that they are five. 'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him that they are Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus, and its apparent meaning is the view that they are four, and this is the most sound of the opinions.

As for the statement of al-Jalal al-Suyuti: that the most sound of them is the view that they are five, these four and our Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him and upon them all. Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted that from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is what is related from Abu Ja'far and Abu 'Abd Allah, among the imams of the Ahl al-Bayt, may God be pleased with them. Some of the eminent scholars versified them, saying:

*The resolute: Noah, and the Friend, the glorified,*
*And Moses, and Jesus, and the Beloved, Muhammad.*

This is based on their being so after the revelation of the verse, and on our Prophet, peace be upon him, following the one commanded to follow. It is not meant that the most sound opinion is that the intended ones in the verse are those five, may God bless and greet them, for that would entail his being commanded, peace be upon him, to be patient as he himself was patient, and that hardly holds. In accordance with this is the statement of Abu al-'Aliya, as transmitted by 'Abd ibn Humayd, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman*, and Ibn 'Asakir from him, that they are three: Noah, Abraham, and Hud, and the Messenger of God ﷺ is the fourth among them. Perhaps the preferable interpretation of the verse is the first opinion, even though "those of resolve" later became specific to those five, peace be upon them, upon being mentioned without qualification, due to their being well known for it, as with the dominant proper names. So it is as if it were said: "Be patient in calling to the truth and enduring hardships in general, as your brother Messengers before you were patient. ﴿And do not seek to hasten [the punishment] for them﴾, meaning for the disbelievers of Mecca, that is, do not ask for its hastening, for it is about to descend upon them. ﴿As if, on the day they see what they are promised﴾ of punishment, ﴿they had not remained [in the world] except an hour of a day﴾, a brief time, ﴿[the duration of] a single hour of a day﴾, because of what they witness of the severity of the punishment and the length of its duration."

Ubayy recited, "[an hour] of the day." His saying, exalted is He, ﴿A notification﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: this with which you have been admonished is a sufficient admonition, or it is a conveyance from the Messenger. Some made the indication refer to the Qur'an or to what has been mentioned of the surah. The interpretation of ﴿a notification﴾ as "a conveyance" was supported by the reading of Abu Mijlaz and Abu Siraj al-Hudhali, "Convey" (*balligh*), in the imperative form addressed to him, peace be upon him, and by the reading of Abu Mijlaz also in one narration, "He conveyed" (*ballagha*), in the past form of the second verbal pattern. Abu Hayyan preferred that the indication refers to the period they remained in, as if it were said: "That hour is their conveyance," just as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿A little enjoyment﴾.

Abu Mijlaz said: "*Balagh*" is a subject whose predicate is His saying, exalted is He, "for them" (*lahum*), which precedes it. So one stops at ﴿and do not seek to hasten﴾, and begins with His saying, exalted is He, "for them," and the comparative sentence is a parenthetical interjection between the subject and the predicate, and the meaning is: for them is a termination and an arrival at a time when the punishment will descend upon them. This is very weak, because of what it contains of separation and contradiction of the apparent sense, since the apparent sense is that "for them" is connected to "seek to hasten." Al-Hasan, Zayd ibn 'Ali, and 'Isa read "*balagha*" in the accusative, by supposing "Convey a conveyance" or "Convey to us a conveyance" or something similar. Al-Hasan also read "*balaghin*" in the genitive, on the basis that it is a qualifier of "day."

﴿So will any be destroyed except the defiant people﴾, those who depart from heeding admonition or from obedience. In the verse is what it contains of threat and warning.

**[p. 36]**

Ibn Muhaysin, as transmitted by Ibn Khalawayh from him, read "*yuhlaku*" with a fatha on the *ya'* and a kasra on the *lam*. Also from him, "*yahlaku*" with a fatha on the *ya'* and the *lam*, and its past form is "*halaka*" with a kasra on the *lam*, which is a dialect. Abu al-Fath said: it is a disliked form. Zayd ibn Thabit read "*nuhliku*" with the first-person plural of majesty, from the causative form, "the people, the defiant ones" in the accusative. This verse, that is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿As if they...﴾ to the end, has come in some reports with an indication that it has a distinctive property among the verses of this surah.

Al-Tabarani transmitted in *al-Du'a'* from Anas, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "When you seek a need and wish that it be granted, say: 'There is no god but God alone, with no partner. The Most High, the Most Great. There is no god but God alone, with no partner. The Forbearing, the Generous. In the name of God, besides whom there is no god, the Living, the Forbearing. Glory be to God, Lord of the Mighty Throne. Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds. As if they, on the day they see it, had not remained except an evening or its morning. As if they, on the day they see what they are promised, had not remained except an hour of a day. A notification. So will any be destroyed except the defiant people. O God, I ask You for the requisites of Your mercy, the resolute causes of Your forgiveness, safety from every sin, the gain of every righteousness, success in Paradise, and deliverance from the Fire. O God, leave for me no sin except that You forgive it, no anxiety except that You relieve it, no debt except that You settle it, and no need of the needs of this world and the Hereafter except that You grant it, by Your mercy, O Most Merciful of the merciful.'"
